activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
The museum docent had told them to gather in the print room at two, which gave Tyson forty minutes to stand in front of a glass case and pretend the pamphlet inside meant something to him. It was a first edition, the label said, of Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790. His essay prompt sat folded in his back pocket: trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800. Since 1800. The pamphlet was ten years too early.

"You're doing the face," said Priya, appearing beside him with her notebook already open. "The face you do when the essay is winning."

"It's not the essay. It's this." He tapped the glass. "Burke. He condemned the whole thing, the label says, for destroying tradition. And that's basically the conservative view of the Revolution, the one everybody after 1800 argued with. But I can't start before 1800. The prompt has a fence around it."

"So don't start with him. Start with the historians."

"Then I'm starting mid-argument. Nobody's going to know what the argument's about." He read the label again, as if it might have edited itself. "He saw it coming, kind of. The book's from 1790, before the worst of it, and he still hated it. That's almost the interesting part."

Priya wrote something down. She had a way of doing that, transcribing other people's crises. "You could preempt the question," she said. "One paragraph up front saying here's the position everyone's reacting to, then jump the fence."

Tyson did not answer, because Mr. Okafor had materialized behind them with his clipboard and his habit of narrating. "Print room, two o'clock, everyone, and no leaning on cases, the provenance of these items is the whole point of the room." He drifted off toward a boy photographing a broadside.

Tyson leaned very slightly, in protest, and then stopped. "It's not a fence," he said. "It's more like a fault line. Burke's the seismic event, and everything after 1800 is people measuring the aftershocks."

"That's going in the essay, isn't it."

"That's going in the essay."

In the print room they sat on folding chairs while Mr. Okafor held up facsimiles and asked questions nobody answered. "Who can tell me why a book from 1790 is relevant to a paper about views after 1800?" Silence, the good kind, the kind that meant thinking or nothing. Priya looked at Tyson. Tyson looked at the facsimile. He thought about raising his hand and then, in a small internal negotiation, decided against it, because half of a good idea is knowing which half isn't done yet.

Afterward, in the corridor by the vending machines, he laid it out for Priya anyway, because she was the only one who would hold still for it. "Say I open with Burke. Not as a source, as a position. He condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, in 1790, and that became the conservative view, the fixed point. Then everybody I'm actually supposed to write about, all the historians after 1800, they're either agreeing with him or knocking him down or doing something weirder, like agreeing with the part about tradition but not the rest. He's not inside my topic. He's the reason my topic exists."

"So lead with him and jump the fence."

"Or I'm wrong and it looks like I can't read a prompt." He fed a dollar into the machine and pressed the button for the pretzels, which had a reputation. The bag did not drop. He pressed it again. "The thing I can't figure out is whether the prompt means since 1800 as a wall or as a lens. Like, am I only writing about people after 1800, or am I writing about how the Revolution looked from after 1800, in which case what came before matters because it's what people were looking past?"

"Both," said Priya. "Or neither. You could ask Okafor."

"I could." He rattled the machine with his shoulder, a move that worked in principle. The bag shifted, considered, and stayed. "But if I ask, he tells me, and then the essay's his position. I'd rather get it wrong on my own terms and find out."

"You'd rather get it wrong?"

"I'd rather it be mine." The bag dropped, finally, with the sound of a small defeat for the vending machine. He tore it open and ate one, looking back down the corridor toward the print room, where the case with Burke's book caught the afternoon light through the glass door. He took out the folded prompt, smoothed it against his knee, and on the back, in pencil, wrote one line: Begin with the man before the fence.

"What's that mean?" Priya asked, reading over his arm.

"It means I start with Burke," Tyson said, "and then I jump."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
story:
The paint on the porch railing was peeling again, and Nicolas's grandfather, who used to repaint it every June, sat in his chair watching Nicolas do it wrong. That was the arrangement now. Nicolas had come for two weeks in July, partly to help, partly because his mother had said the word "stroke" so quietly at Easter that he'd had to ask her to say it again. The stroke had taken most of Grandpa's words. What it had left was a right hand that still worked and a face that seemed, to Nicolas, more phlegmatic than ever, as if decades of titrations had trained it to show nothing until the evidence was in.

Nicolas had brought his chemistry notebook, the one with the exam schedule folded inside, because he was retaking the test in August. On the porch, between coats of paint, he read about equilibrium and felt the familiar sense that the universe was cheating. A reaction could go forward and backward at once. Adding heat, the book said, shifted the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. He'd underlined it twice and understood it not at all. Why couldn't heat just speed everything up equally, the way his father claimed coffee sped up his mother equally in every direction, which was a joke Nicolas had heard lambasted at enough dinners to last a lifetime.

In the kitchen that evening he found the old shelf of jars, and among them a bottle of cobalt chloride, blue crystals, older than he was. Grandpa had been a chemist at the plant forty years, back when the plant existed. Nicolas remembered, from before, the trick with the paper strips that turned pink in humid air, and how Grandpa would hold one to his lips and breathe on it like a fortune teller. He dissolved a pinch in water and got a pale violet, an in-between color, and wrote in his notebook, solution not blue or pink, in between. He put half in one glass and half in another.

He set a saucepan of water on the stove and filled a bowl from the tap with ice from the freezer, the ice cubes clattering like dropped coins. Grandpa wheeled his chair to the doorway and watched. Nicolas lowered one glass into the hot water and the other into the ice, and crouched so both were level with his eyes. "Watch," he said, though he wasn't sure whether he was saying it to Grandpa or to himself.

The glass in the ice water pinkened first, slowly, like a cheek in January. The one in the saucepan took longer, then darkened glass by glass toward blue, and Nicolas understood something with his eyes before he could say it with his mouth, that the color was telling him which way the equilibrium had shifted, pink one way, blue the other, and that the shift had a direction, that it could be pushed. He pulled both glasses out and set them on the counter, side by side, pink and blue, and the middle color he'd started with existed nowhere anymore.

"Equilibrium," he said. Grandpa's mouth twitched, which was how he applauded now. Nicolas sat on the floor with his back against the cabinet, because the thought arrived better at that altitude. "Okay, but here's what I don't get." He held up the blue glass. "Heat is speed. The book says heat speeds up reactions. So it should speed up both reactions, the forward one and the backward one, equally, and everything just happens faster in both directions and nothing changes. But it changes. It goes blue." He looked at the two glasses, then at his grandfather, who looked back with the patience of a man who had watched a thousand solutions change color and was willing to watch the boy change his mind.

Grandpa raised the working hand and made a small gesture, fingers apart, one hand tilted. Not equal. Nicolas sat with that. Not equal. "It speeds up both," he said slowly. "Forward and reverse. But not the same. It speeds up the endothermic direction more, the one that takes heat in, like it's feeding it, so that's the direction that wins, and the whole equilibrium shifts that way." He said it a second time, quieter, testing it, and it held. That was the thing nobody had told him, that the shift wasn't heat choosing a side, it was heat being uneven, and the unevenness was the shift. Grandpa nodded once, a nod so small it might have been gravity, and Nicolas wrote it down under the two colors, and his pencil broke on the last word, and he laughed, and Grandpa laughed too, or made the sound where laughter had been.

They left the glasses on the counter overnight. In the morning Nicolas found them both back at violet, both drifted home to the middle, the shift undone the moment the ice melted and the pan cooled. He stood there with the morning light flat on the counter and felt the small ache underneath the triumph, that he would retake the exam in August and probably pass it, and that Grandpa, who had known all of this once and could no longer say any of it, had watched the color change and could only tilt his hand.

At breakfast the radio said something about the economy, and Grandpa tapped the table at the word stagflation, twice, the way he used to at dinner when the news confirmed some opinion of his, and Nicolas, who didn't know exactly what the word meant, poured the coffee anyway. Then he went out to the porch with the paint can, and Grandpa followed in his chair, and Nicolas started on the second coat over the first, which was still tacky, and Grandfa raised his hand and stopped him.

"Not yet," Nicolas guessed.

Grandpa shook his head and pointed at the railing, then at Nicolas, then spread his fingers slowly apart. Wait for it to shift. Nicolas set the brush down on the lid of the can and sat on the steps beside him, and they watched the paint dry together.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
I don't get nervous at tournaments anymore, which is one of the things people say about me that happens to be true, and I had plenty of time that Saturday to prove it. My round wasn't for another hour, the hallway of Whitfield High smelled like floor wax and someone's microwaved ramen, and I was sitting outside Room 114 with my flow pad on my knees, not thinking about my affirmative case at all. I was thinking about the one-act. This is the part that's hard to explain to people: I signed up to direct a play for the spring festival knowing almost nothing about directing, the same way I signed up for debate four years ago knowing almost nothing about argument, and both times everyone acted like I'd made a reasonable choice.

The one-act was Pinter's "Trouble in the Works," twenty minutes of a man complaining to a foreman about machine parts with names like "grunge splitters." I had cast Dev as Filer, the complainer, because Dev could talk, and honestly that was the whole criterion. My co-director, Priya, had wanted to run blocking rehearsals by drawing arrows on a ground plan like a football coach. I told her arrows were for people who didn't trust their actors. She told me that was the most debate-brained sentence she'd ever heard. I still maintain she said it with respect.

That morning I'd told her I'd be at the tournament by nine and rehearsal by two, no problem. My partner Marcus had dropped at the last minute, food poisoning, the kind of convenient illness I chose not to interrogate because I wanted to solo anyway. Soloists get to control the whole round. I'm aware of how that sounds. Priya texted me twice during cross-examination prep, which I ignored, and a third time during my round, which I also ignored, though I told her later my phone had been in my bag.

I won the round, or the judge said I did, and I've decided to count those as the same thing. What actually mattered was the hour after. I found the empty cafeteria annex where the drama kids had set up a rehearsal space, tape on the floor marking the edge of a stage that didn't exist yet, folding chairs in three ragged rows to stand in for the audience. Priya was there. Dev was there, and the other kid, Ben, playing the foreman, a freshman with incipient sideburns he was clearly proud of. They had started without me. I stood by the vending machines and watched for a while before anyone noticed.

Here's what I saw, and I want to be accurate because Priya says I exaggerate. Dev and Ben had parked themselves in profile, facing each other across a taped square like two lawyers at a podium, and for whole stretches of the scene all I could see of Dev was the back of his head. His voice carried fine. He was funny, even, the part where he complains about the "unlunging bearings" got a laugh from Priya. But the laugh felt like it was arriving by accident, aimed at a wall I couldn't see past. In debate you learn to interpolate between what a judge writes on the ballot and what they actually meant, and I was doing that now with the empty chairs, trying to imagine an audience behind them receiving only hair.

I said, "Rotate a little. Cheat out."

Priya turned. "You know that word?"

"It means you turn partly toward the audience even when you're talking to the other guy," I said. "So your face and voice carry." I'd read it the night before at one in the morning, in a used bookstore copy of a stagecraft manual, one paragraph, and I'd absorbed it the way you absorb a card you know will win a round. I wasn't going to admit the timeline.

Dev angled his shoulders maybe thirty degrees toward the chairs and kept his eyes on Ben, and the difference was embarrassing in its size. His whole performance was suddenly available. He wasn't cheating at all; the honesty of him looking at Ben stayed, and we could still see it happen. Ben copied him without being told. The scene got better in a way I had nothing to do with, which Priya pointed out, and I let her.

We ran it twice more. Between runs she argued that blocking should be fixed before intent, since movement shapes meaning, and I argued the reverse, and I noticed, somewhere in the middle of constructing my second rebuttal, that I didn't fully believe either position. That's the thing debate never taught me: in a round you have to collapse the question, pick a side, because the ballot has only two signatures on it. Directing didn't want a winner. Directing wanted both claims true at once, arrows on the ground plan and trust in the actors, and if there was a teleology to a rehearsal it wasn't winning, it was the moment twenty minutes from now when Dev's face would be visible to strangers in the dark.

I got back to the annex at two, exactly as I'd promised Priya I would, only two hours later than she'd expected me. Dev was stretched out on the folding chairs with his script over his face. "We're going again," I said. "From the top, and everybody cheat out."

He lifted the pages and looked at me for a long second. "Fine," he said. "But I want my chair moved downstage first."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
Brayden's grandfather was convalescing in the back bedroom of the house where Brayden now studied, which meant every hour or so the study lamp burned late over a borrowed textbook while the oxygen concentrator hummed down the hall. The planetarium had a test on Friday. Pass it, and Brayden would run the Saturday climate show himself, a real microphone, a real dome, instead of sweeping the rows between presentations. He had copied the graph onto graph paper twice, carbon dioxide climbing across the last century in a line that looked almost polite in its steadiness, and underneath it he had written his best guess at why the air was warming: the most abundant gases must be doing the trapping.

His cousin Priya found the page on Tuesday night. She had come to drop off soup for their grandfather and stayed to steal the desk lamp's warmth, her own chemistry homework spread across the rug, a worksheet on enthalpy with half the problems circled in pencil. She read Brayden's sentence upside down, then right side up, then laughed in a way that made him put his pen down.

"Read it again," she said. "Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air."

"So they're most of the air."

"And they are not greenhouse gases." She tapped the textbook's margin, where the sentence sat in small print he had skimmed past. "Molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation."

He stared at the line. "That's backwards from what I said."

"That's exactly what I said."

The argument lasted through two bowls of soup eaten cold at the desk. Brayden argued that it couldn't work that way, that the stuff there was most of had to matter most, and Priya kept dragging her finger back to the same sentence without raising her voice, which was worse than shouting. When their grandfather called out that the soup was good, they both went quiet, and in the quiet Brayden copied the sentence word for word into his notes and found that copying it did not feel like understanding it. He sat with that feeling. He underlined nothing.

By Thursday he could explain it out loud in the planetarium's empty theater, saying "not greenhouse gases" to the tilted dome the way he would say it to a Saturday crowd, and he had learned to read the graph with a ruler laid along the curve, showing where the line bent and where it did not. The dome smelled of carpet dust and the cold metal of the armrests; the projector sat torpid at the room's center, dark, waiting for someone to give it something to say. His supervisor, Ms. Okafor, had left a practice question on the console: why does a small fraction of the air matter so much for heat. Brayden wrote his answer in the margin and did not write the wrong sentence anywhere, not even to cross it out.

On Friday she tested him under the half-lit dome. She ran the slides and he talked, and when the carbon dioxide graph appeared, huge and slow, he laid the ruler against the screen's edge without being asked, tracing the climb with the words coming steadier than he expected. Then she said, "A kid asks you why the whole sky isn't a blanket, then. Ninety-nine percent of it. What do you tell him?"

Brayden heard his own pause in the microphone, amplified, a small breath the whole dome could hear.

"I'd tell him nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases," he said, "because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation." He let it sit, then added, "And I'd say the sky is mostly made of things that let the heat through, and a small part of it doesn't, and that small part is what we made bigger."

Ms. Okafor looked at him for a moment longer than the answer required. "You hesitated."

"I was checking whether I still believed the wrong version. I did, for three days."

She signed the sheet and slid it across the console. "Saturday, ten o'clock. The ruler stays."

That night Brayden drove back to his grandfather's house with the signed page on the passenger seat. Priya was there again, soup containers stacked in the sink, her enthalpy worksheet finally finished, its circled problems crossed out one by one. He put the page in front of her without a word.

"Ten o'clock Saturday," she read. She looked up. "Do it for me. The whole thing."

He stood in the dim kitchen, faced the window where the dark yard stood in for the dome, laid an invisible ruler against an invisible graph, and began.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
Laura had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the good light and an outlet that actually worked, and she spread her materials across it like evidence at a trial: two legal pads, a binder of clippings, a printed copy of a Supreme Court opinion with more highlighter on it than plain paper. In three days she would stand before a panel of local lawyers in the county courthouse's moot courtroom and argue both sides of a case about a student suspended for wearing a shirt the principal called disruptive. Both sides. The rules of the competition demanded it, and the demand felt to Laura like being asked to shake hands with someone mid-argument.

She had started with the side she believed, obviously, the student's side, and she had found the line she needed within an hour. It came from a 1969 case called Tinker v. Des Moines, about students who wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War. The Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate. She read the sentence aloud to the empty chair across from her, quietly, the way she practiced openings. It had the ring of something that would stay with the judges.

"The schoolhouse gate," said a voice. "You're doing Tinker?"

The boy from her civics class, Marcus, stood at the end of the table with a stack of books and a coffee he clearly shouldn't have brought past the front desk. He did mock trial too, at the other high school across town, though she'd only seen him at the library, always at the microfilm machine like some kind of historian.

"For my rebuttal," Laura said. "It's a dress-code case, and it's the most famous line about student speech there is."

"It's famous for a reason," Marcus said, setting his books down without asking. "Can I hear your other side? Everyone forgets the other side."

She hadn't forgotten it. She had been avoiding it with a discipline that felt almost physical, the way you avoid a loose tooth. The other side was that a school was not a public square, that thirteen hundred teenagers in one building created problems the founders never imagined, that the principal had a duty to keep the day moving. She had written one paragraph of it and it read like a betrayal.

"I have it," she said.

"Read it to me."

She read it. It was short, and it was bad, and Marcus didn't bother to hide his wince. "You argued it like you were apologizing for it," he said. "The judges will hear that in the first sentence. You have to find the version of that argument you actually believe."

"That's the problem. There isn't one."

"There is," he said. "You just haven't had to look yet. Try this. If a kid wears a shirt that makes half the cafeteria unable to think about anything else, who pays the cost? Not the kid. The kid chose it. The cost lands on everybody else's education. That's the whole idea of utilitarianism, right, the greatest good, and in a building with a captive audience of thirteen hundred, the principal's the only one counting."

Laura wrote it down before she could decide whether she agreed, because it was better than her paragraph and she knew it. "That's still just majority convenience over one person's rights," she said.

"Maybe. Or maybe school is the one place where you're forced to be there, so the normal rules about walking away don't apply. That's what the dissent was getting at, sort of. Two justices didn't buy it, remember. It was 7-2, not unanimous."

She looked at him. "You've read the dissents."

"I like the dissents." He shrugged, almost truculent about it, chin up like he expected her to laugh. "Everyone quotes the gate. Nobody reads what the two said on the other side of it."

They worked until the light through the window turned from white to gold. He made her argue the school's side to him for twenty straight minutes, playing a doubtful judge, interrupting with questions she couldn't answer and making her find the answers out loud. Once, when she found a phrase that landed, a version of the captive-audience argument that actually sounded like law, she felt something she could only describe as being enraptured by her own position, and then immediately uneasy about it, the way you're uneasy when you catch yourself enjoying an argument you're supposed to dislike.

By closing time she had two openings written, one for each side, and both of them were good. That was the part she hadn't expected, that she could hold both and not feel split down the middle. She believed the student had the better case. She also believed a principal standing in a hallway at 7:40 in the morning, watching a disruption build, had a real problem that the law hadn't fully solved, and she couldn't say where the line fell between them. She could only say where it had fallen once, in 1969, by a vote of 7-2, and that the line had been argued about every year since.

On the night of the competition, the courtroom was fuller than she'd expected, and the panel turned out to be three attorneys and a sitting judge with a reputation for being merciless. Laura argued the student's side first, and the Tinker line landed exactly the way she'd practiced, the schoolhouse gate, the 7-2 ruling, constitutional rights that students carry with them through the door, and she watched one of the attorneys nod.

Then she switched to the school's side, took a breath, and began the argument she had built with Marcus at the library table, and somewhere in the middle of the captive-audience point she realized she was winning, genuinely winning, panel leaning forward, judge's pen moving.

When the scores came back, the student side had taken second. The school's side, the one she'd fought against for weeks, had taken first.

Her mother found her afterward by the water fountain. "So which one did you actually believe?" she asked.

Laura looked past her at the judge gathering his papers, and said, "Ask me tomorrow."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Eva sat in the empty chemistry lab after last period, staring at the retake slip Mrs. Okafor had handed her. Forty-eight hours, one more chance on the DNA unit, and she still could not keep the words straight. She had written "translation happens first" on the quiz, and Mrs. Okafor had circled it twice, which felt like being circled by a predator.

Marcus from her class plopped down across the table with his notes spread like a card trick. "I made you a deal," he said. "You quiz me on the enzymes, I quiz you on the order of things."

"Fine. RNA polymerase."

"What it does," Marcus said, tapping his pen. "That's where you fell apart. Go."

She tried. "It... copies everything? Both strands?"

Marcus winced. "That would be a travesty of the whole process. You'd get two copies tangled together." He slid his paper toward her. On it he had drawn a ladder, then a single rail peeling away with letters marching off it. He pointed, but he did not explain, which was annoying, because explaining was the entire point of a study partner.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Her little cousin Dani, calling from the farm in a panic about her own science homework, sixth grade, a worksheet due tomorrow. "It's asking why the cell doesn't just send the DNA out to make stuff," Dani said, the sound of chickens behind her. "That's the whole question. It makes no sense."

Eva looked at Marcus's drawing. Something clicked into place, the way a key turns after you've been forcing it wrong. "You know how at the library you don't lend out the original of something?" she said. "You make a copy and send the copy."

"The worksheet says a word," Dani said. "Transcription."

"Right, transcription." Eva traced the rail on Marcus's drawing with her finger, holding the phone against her shoulder. "In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. One strand, not both. And the messenger RNA carries the gene's instructions out. So the original stays safe in the nucleus, like the library book, and the copy goes out and does the work."

There was a pause, then Dani said, "Ohhh. That's actually smart," and Eva felt something settle in her own head, the nascent understanding finally standing up on its own legs. She had explained it without hesitating, and in explaining it she had understood it. She hung up and looked at Marcus. "Say the thing again. The matching strand part."

"Matching strand of messenger RNA," he said. "It carries the gene's instructions. You just told your cousin the whole thing."

"I did, didn't I." She pulled the retake slip out of her pocket and smoothed it on the table. "Okay. Quiz me. Hard."

He went through it three times, and each time she got faster. When she said "RNA polymerase" without stumbling, Marcus did a small drumroll on the table with his knuckles, and the lab technician across the hall looked in through the window with an expression that did not augur much patience for students still in the building at five o'clock.

The next morning Eva sat in Mrs. Okafor's room with the retake in front of her. The question asked her to trace the path from gene to protein, in order, with names. She wrote transcription first, then drew the ladder and the single rail peeling away, then the messenger RNA leaving with its copied instructions, then the ribosome reading it, translation, amino acids snapping together. Her hand was steady. When she got to the last line she thought of Dani at the farm, probably turning in her worksheet with chickens shouting in the background, and she smiled without meaning to.

Mrs. Okafor collected the papers and flipped through them at her desk while Eva gathered her bag. She paused on one page, then looked up. "Whatever you did between Tuesday and today," she said, "keep doing it."

Eva shouldered her bag. "I called a farmer," she said.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
The fluorescent lights above aisle six made everything look slightly ill, the oranges especially, and Nevaeh stood under them with two folded lease agreements in the front pocket of her hoodie, waiting for her mother to finish arguing with the coupon machine. The machine had eaten another quarter. This was the third time. Her mother slapped its side with the flat of her hand the way she slapped the dryer at home, and Nevaeh looked away, because looking away was easier than watching.

The leases belonged to her brother, Dorian, who was twenty and moving out of Aunt Cece's basement in eleven days. But Dorian worked nights stocking the same warehouse where their mother worked days, and he had handed the papers to Nevaeh at breakfast with a shrug that meant you do the math, you're the smart one. She had accepted the shrug the way she accepted most things from Dorian, silently, and then spent two evenings with a calculator and a growing suspicion that neither apartment was possible.

The first apartment, on Peralta Street, rented for nine hundred and forty a month, utilities not included. The second, out past the community college, was eleven hundred and twenty, utilities included. It had taken her most of one evening just to find out what utilities meant in practice, because the Peralta landlord's listing said "tenant pays all utilities," which turned out to mean electric, gas, water, trash, and internet, each billed separately, each with its own deposit. She had called the water company pretending to be a tenant and written the numbers on the back of a receipt.

At the store she pushed the cart while her mother dropped in the cheap peanut butter, the dented cans, the bread that was two days from expiring and therefore forty percent off. Nevaeh had been reading the backs of her mother's choices for years, the way other kids read cereal boxes, and she could metabolize a unit price in seconds now, cost per ounce, cost per sheet, cost per calorie. It was the same skill, she realized, standing in front of the rice, that she was applying to the apartments. What she had never done was apply it to their own household, and the realization had a seismic quality, a slow shifting under what she had assumed was solid ground.

"You're quiet," her mother said at the meat counter, where she bought one package of chicken thighs and put back a second.

"I'm doing Dorian's math. The apartments."

Her mother made a sound that could have meant anything. Nevaeh laid it out anyway, in the checkout line, on top of the moving belt. Peralta came to roughly eleven hundred a month once she added the utility estimates. The other place was eleven twenty flat. Nearly identical. "So it's not even a choice," she said. "The second one's better. Everything's included, nothing can jump up on him."

Her mother fed the coupon machine one last quarter, won, and exhaled. "What does he make? At the warehouse."

"About nineteen hundred a month. If the hours hold."

Her mother did not say anything for the length of the belt, the scanner beeping, the total climbing. Then she said, "There's a word for that, you know. More than thirty percent of income on housing. They call it cost-burdened. It's a government thing. Your aunt told me when we were looking for this place." She took the bags in both arms. "He'd be paying more than half."

Nevaeh stood there while the numbers rearranged themselves. She had been comparing the two leases as though they were two brands of rice, cheaper against cheaper, but the real comparison was between either lease and her brother's paycheck, and on that scale both failed, badly, identically. Sixty percent. She said the percentage out loud in the parking lot, holding the cart while her mother loaded the trunk, and heard how it sounded, and stopped saying it.

In the car, the phonetics of it stayed with her, the word her mother had used, burden, how blunt it was, no softer syllable in it anywhere. She watched the store shrink in the side mirror and understood something she could not yet put into a sentence: that she had learned to compare two things and discovered that the comparison was beside the point. Dorian needed a third option that did not exist in his folder, or a raise, or a roommate, and she did not know how to calculate any of those. At home she found him awake in the kitchen, and she put both leases on the table in front of him, and said, "Before you sign either one, sit down with me and bring your last three pay stubs."

story:
The laundromat on Mill Street had one working socket by the folding table, so Naomi claimed it the way her grandmother claimed territory on the steppe of her imagination, wide and without negotiation, spreading leases, a calculator, and a phone charger across the plastic surface while the dryer thumped behind her. Two flats, two landlords, one September start at a university she had not yet visited. Flat A was four hundred and sixty pounds a month, bills not included, eleven minutes from campus by the admissions officer's optimistic estimate. Flat B was five hundred and forty, water included, gas and electric separate, and it had a window seat in the photos that she kept returning to even though window seats did not appear in any calculation she knew how to do.

Her mother had said, before handing over the folder of printed paperwork, "Read the small print twice." Her brother had said, "Just pick the cheaper one, Naoms, it's a flat, not a marriage." Neither of them had said how to compare two things that differed in every particular, and so she sat in the fluorescent hum with a damp sock on her knee and began, methodically, to make it worse.

The dryer stopped. She fed it more coins, and while the machine swallowed them a man about her father's age began folding shirts at the other end of the table, glancing at her papers the way people glance at accidents. "Rent comparison?" he said. "My daughter did that last year. Took her a week."

"It's taking me a week too," Naomi said. "The problem is I don't know what a month costs. One includes water, one includes nothing, and the listings just say 'utilities estimated.' Estimated by whom? Optimists?"

"Landlords," he said, and they both laughed, quietly, the laugh of people who had recently been eighteen and could see eighteen from where they stood.

She built the total for each flat on paper, line by line, averaging the utilities the listing agents had cheerfully guessed at, adding the internet she would need, the bus pass for Flat B since it sat farther out. Flat A came to something near six hundred a month all in. Flat B came to six hundred and forty. The window seat cost forty pounds, she wrote, and then crossed that out because sentiment was not a line item, or shouldn't be, though she privately decided to predicate her final choice partly on it anyway, because a person was allowed to want one beautiful thing if she was honest that she was paying for it.

Then she reached the deposit clauses, and the two flats stopped resembling each other entirely. Flat A's landlord wanted eleven hundred pounds up front, refundable, "held against damages." Flat B wanted eight hundred. Her savings covered either, barely, but not both a deposit and a first month's rent at Flat A, which would have left her eating whatever her mother mailed in boxes. She was typing the phrase how much deposit can a landlord charge uk into her phone when the folding man leaned over, not reading her papers now but clearly deciding whether to speak.

"My daughter's landlord tried that," he said. "There's a cap. Five weeks' rent, that's the most they can take, if the yearly rent is under fifty thousand pounds. Over fifty thousand, it's six weeks." He picked up another shirt, shook it out. "Look it up, don't take my word."

She looked it up. The council pages said the same thing in the same flat arithmetic: five weeks' rent where the annual rent came to less than fifty thousand pounds, six weeks where it reached that figure or crossed it. Her flats were both far under the line, which meant both caps were five weeks. Eleven hundred pounds was more than five weeks of four hundred and sixty; she worked it out twice, because being wrong about money her mother did not have to spare was not an option. The Flat A landlord was over the limit, and by a margin she could name. Eight hundred against five weeks of five hundred and forty came in just under. Flat B was legal; Flat A was not.

Here was the part nobody had warned her about: the numbers had rearranged the question. Flat B, the more expensive flat, was now somehow the safer one, and Flat A had revealed something about its landlord that no spreadsheet could calculate back away. She drafted a message to the Flat A agent, circumspect in her phrasing, asking only whether the deposit figure was correct as written, and set the phone face down on the table while the dryer thumped into its second hour. The man with the shirts had left a folded tower of laundry and a receipt on which he'd scrawled, in ballpoint, good luck, and under it a small drawing of a chair. She didn't know if he meant the window seat. She looked at the drying window of Flat B's photo on her screen, then at the sent message sitting in the Flat A inbox, unreplied, and began pulling her warm clothes from the drum one sleeve at a time.

story:
Ava was hiding in the surgery prep room again, flashcards fanned across the counter beside a bottle of betadine, when Dr. Okafor's dog started coding in kennel four. She was supposed to be studying for her cell bio placement exam, the one that would decide whether she could skip the intro lecture and take the smaller seminar in her first semester, and instead she was listening to the clock by the gurney and mouthing the steps of cellular respiration like a prayer she half remembered. Glycolysis. The link reaction. The citric acid cycle. Then the part she could never keep straight, the electron transport chain, which her textbook had drawn as a row of lumps in a membrane like stones in a stream.

The dog was old, a settershepherd mix named Biscuit with a heart that had been failing since spring, and the technicians moved around Ava as though she were a piece of equipment. She watched them bag him, watched the monitor stutter, and she thought about her father, who had sat in this same clinic two years ago with their cat Mango's carrier on his knees while the vet explained what a peaceful end looked like. Ava had been sixteen then, and she had said yes to the euthanasia without letting her father finish the sentence, because she could not stand the silence where the explanation was supposed to go. She had wondered since whether she'd agreed too fast, whether deciding quickly was mercy or just cowardice wearing mercy's coat.

"Glucose to pyruvate," she whispered, shuffling cards. "Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA." One of the techs, Marisol, backed through the door with a bag of fluids and said, "If you're going to mutter, mutter something useful, like my ex-husband's address." Ava laughed, and the laugh loosened something, and she said the next step out loud: electrons.

Here was her problem, the actual problem, the one underneath the exam. Her textbook and her flashcards disagreed. The cards, which she'd bought secondhand from a girl in a cosmopolitan study group who had covered them in annotations, said the oxygen you breathed became energy. The book said no such thing. It said the oxygen sat at the end of the electron transport chain, in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and accepted electrons, and combined with protons, and became water. Ava had read that sentence nine times. It refused to become intuitive. Energy felt like fire, like fuel burning; water felt like a byproduct, something you expelled. The two frameworks sat in her like two people at a party pretending not to know each other.

She had tried to force it earlier that week by transliterating her notes into what she called "kitchen language": glucose was the dough, ATP was the finished bread, the mitochondria were the oven. That worked until she hit oxygen, because oxygen wasn't an ingredient you could taste in the bread; it was something about the oven itself, the draft, the flame under the coils. She'd gotten tangled and angry and had written, in the margin, "ASK SOMEONE WHO ISN'T MAKING THIS UP." But there was no one to ask. Her mother was a nurse who understood patients, not membranes. Her father still couldn't say the word euthanasia out loud.

In kennel four, the monitor steadied. Biscuit was going to live through the afternoon at least, and Dr. Okafor came out pulling off her gloves and saw the flashcards and said, "Electron transport chain? God, I haven't thought about that since 1994." She leaned on the counter, tired in a satisfied way, and looked at Ava's margin note and raised an eyebrow.

Ava explained, feeling like a fraud, that she couldn't make the oxygen make sense, that her cards said oxygen became energy and the book said something about water. Dr. Okafor did not lecture. She only tapped Biscuit's chart, where a fluid bag was noted, where a nasal cannula had been noted, and said, "What's in that fluid bag, mostly?"

"Water," Ava said.

"And what was on his face?"

"Oxygen."

Dr. Okafor went back to her patient, and Ava stood there with her mouth slightly open, because she could see it suddenly, not as a diagram but as a fact inside a body: the oxygen Biscuit had breathed in had ended up as water inside him, inside his cells, in the inner mitochondrial membrane where the chain ended and the oxygen took the electrons and took the protons and made water. The oxygen she herself was breathing, the oxygen her father had breathed in the waiting room while Mango's heart slowed, all of it destined for the same quiet conversion. It was not fuel. It was a place where something was received. She did not yet fully understand the difference between those two ideas, but she understood that the difference mattered, and she wrote on a fresh card, in her own handwriting this time, "O2 is the final electron acceptor. It combines with H+ to form water. Breathe in, become part of yourself."

She thought about enthalpy for half a second, the word from her chemistry teacher, energy contained and released, and about whether her quick yes two years ago had released something for her father or only contained it. She could not decide, and she noticed that she did not need to decide tonight, that some judgments could be carried like flashcards in a back pocket, worn soft from handling, answers still pending. She squared the deck, put it in her scrubs, and went to help Marisol carry Biscuit, breathing and heavy and wet-nosed, out to the car.

story:
The smell of the clinic was antiseptic underneath and dog on top, and Alexis had stopped noticing either by her second Saturday of volunteering. What she noticed now was the waiting room's plastic chairs, where she had spread her biology notes across three of them, and the diagram of a mitochondrion she had drawn twice already because the first one looked like a jelly bean with regrets.

"You're off duty until the Pattersons get here," said Rosa, the technician with the gray braid, passing through with a stack of towels. "So be off duty somewhere less visible."

Alexis gathered her things into the exam room where the kennels were, where it was warm and the beagles snored in stacked cages. Her test was Monday. Cellular respiration, glycolysis to ATP, the whole winding road of it, and she still could not keep the order straight. Last night the group chat had collapsed into an argument. Devon insisted the first carbon dioxide came out of the Krebs cycle. Priya said no, it was earlier, it was when pyruvate got processed, though she couldn't say where that happened, and Devon had typed three laughing emojis and the word "guessing," which Priya did not deserve. Priya had been the one who stayed late after the last test to help Alexis with enzymes, and Alexis had watched her get vilified in the chat for a half-remembered answer, and said nothing. She had typed "lol" and closed the app. That was Friday. It sat in her like a swallowed stone.

She read the chapter again, slowly this time, the way Priya read, one finger under each line. Glycolysis happened in the cytoplasm, outside, and it split glucose into two pyruvates, and no carbon dioxide left anything. That much she was sure of. So Devon's claim depended on the Krebs cycle being the first place carbon left the molecule. She turned the page.

The beagle in cage four lifted its head, yawned, and settled again, phlegmatic about everything, including its overnight stay. Down the hall a door opened, and Rosa's voice rose with it, then another voice, higher, cracked at the edges.

"His name is Biscuit," the woman was saying when Alexis leaned out. "He's breathing funny. He was fine this morning."

Rosa took the little dog, a dachshund with a barrel chest and rapid, shallow breaths, and carried him past. Alexis caught the vet, Dr. Okafor, already in scrubs though it was her day off, and then the door of the back room swung shut and there was nothing to do but go back to her chair. Her phone buzzed. Priya: did you figure out the co2 thing? devon is still being devon.

She typed and deleted three replies. She didn't want to answer until she was sure, and she was aware that this was a decision too, that waiting could look like loyalty or like cowardice depending on how the answer landed. She went back to the diagram.

The chapter moved the pyruvate out of the cytoplasm and into the mitochondrion, into the matrix, which she made herself label on her drawing, the innermost space, past both membranes. And there it was, a sentence she must have skimmed three times without seeing: in the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide. Before the Krebs cycle ever began. Before Devon's answer. She read it again, then a third time, then looked up Krebs in the index just to confirm the order of operations, that the cycle took acetyl-CoA as its starting material, which meant the conversion had to come first, which meant Priya was right and had been right while being laughed at.

"In the mitochondrial matrix," she said out loud, to the beagle, to the warm room. "Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and one carbon dioxide comes off right there."

The beagle thumped its tail once against the cage floor, which she chose to take as corroboration.

She thought about how sure Devon had sounded. That was the thing about him, the erudition was real, mostly, but the confidence ran ahead of it, and the rest of them followed the confidence. She had followed it herself, on the enzymes question, and had gotten it wrong on paper and worse than wrong in the chat. She pulled the phone toward her and then pushed it back, because there was still the question of how to say it. Not whether to say it. She'd settled that, or mostly settled it; the part she hadn't settled was whether she was doing this for Priya or for the pleasure of being right at Devon's expense, and she suspected it was some of each and that the mixture mattered.

The back-room door opened. Rosa came out with her braid coming loose and her face tired in a way Alexis hadn't seen on her before. "The dog's staying," she said. "Oxygen cage, overnight watch. He's stable."

"What was wrong with him?" Alexis asked.

Rosa rubbed the back of her neck. "We'll know more after bloodwork. Right now it's breathing and watching." She looked at the notes spread across the chair, the jelly bean mitochondrion, the arrows. "Any of that make sense yet?"

"Part of it," Alexis said. "The part where the cell breaks things down and gets energy back out. It's all steps. You can't skip one or the whole thing stalls."

"Like a clinic," Rosa said, and went to call the owners.

Alexis picked up the phone. She typed: it's not the krebs cycle. it happens before, when pyruvate turns into acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, and one CO2 comes off right there. i checked the book. she hovered, then added: sorry i didn't say anything last night. She sent it before she could weigh it further, and the weighing kept going anyway, the way Biscuit's breathing had gone on in the back room, quick and small and unobservable from here.

Then she began drawing the matrix again, this time careful, both membranes labeled, and wrote pyruvate at the border with an arrow going in, and beside it, small and exact, one CO2 going out.

story:
Sebastian had signed up to co-teach the wellness workshop because Priya dared him to, and now the workshop was tomorrow at nine, and the only thing he knew for certain was that he did not want to stand in front of thirty sophomores and say something a doctor would have to correct later. That was what the appointment was for, ostensibly. His mother had made it in April for a physical before soccer season, and the receptionist had let him reschedule it for the Thursday before, which happened to put him in a beige exam room two days before he had to explain consent, contraception and where to get tested for infections to a roomful of teenagers who would laugh at the word condom and then go quiet in a way that meant they were listening.

"So what brings you in today," the nurse practitioner said, typing. "Beyond the form."

He told her. He told her about the workshop, and the packets the health office had given him, and how the word consent looked simple on paper until he tried to say it out loud in his dorm room, rehearsing, and heard how much he was leaving out. The nurse, whose badge said D. Okafor, swiveled her chair away from the screen.

"Good," she said. "Most people your age can't define it. Try."

He tried. "It's when both people want it, and say so, and either one can change their mind." He paused. "And it has to be free, not traded. Not 'if you loved me.'"

"And how do you know someone wants it if they don't say it out loud?"

"You ask," he said. "And you believe the answer." He was surprised by how firm it sounded, and then less surprised when he remembered whose voice he was borrowing: Priya's, from an argument in October that had ended better than it began.

Then Okafor flipped his folder shut and asked whether he had questions he was too embarrassed to ask, and he did, one, and it had been sitting in him since Priya started the pill in January like a stone at the bottom of a creek where the water ran too turbid to see it. He had assumed, all these months, that the pill simply worked. He'd read "over 99 percent effective" on some website and stopped reading there.

"I keep seeing ninety-nine percent," he said. "For the pill. Is that a lie?"

"That's perfect use," she said. She wrote nothing down for once. "Typical use is different. With typical use, about seven in a hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, and often that's because doses get missed."

He sat with the number. Seven in a hundred. Not one. He thought of the mornings Priya texted him from the bathroom mirror, phone balanced on the sink, alarm going off at 7:10 so she'd remember, and the mornings after exam weeks when she said she'd taken it late, sheepish, and he'd said it was fine because he genuinely believed it was fine. He had been reassuring her with a number he hadn't checked.

"Why do you stress the alarm, then," he said. "The daily reminder thing. In your handouts."

"Because the gap between perfect and typical is mostly missed doses," Okafor said. "That's the whole reason I harp on it." She looked at him steadily. "You're not asking for the packet."

He exhaled. "My girlfriend's been on it since January. She misses it sometimes. Not a lot. I told her it was fine."

"Is it fine?"

"I don't know," he said. "That's the honest answer. It's better than nothing, and it's not what I thought it was, and I don't know where in between we are." He noticed he was gripping the edge of the exam table, the paper crinkling under his thumbs, and made himself let go. He thought of October again, the fight about whether he'd actually listened when she said she wasn't sure, and how he'd apologized without fully understanding what for. The chronology of that night still embarrassed him: her saying no softly, him not stopping fast enough, the talk afterward, the slow repair. He had learned consent the hard way and then taught himself to speak it fluently, and now he was learning the rest of the vocabulary late.

Okafor gave him a card with the clinic's hours for STI testing, walk-in, no parental note needed, and said, "Nobody there will stigmatize you for asking. That's the entire point of the place." She said the pill number again so he'd have it right, seven in a hundred with typical use, often missed doses, and made him repeat it back.

He walked out through the waiting room with the card in his pocket and called Priya from the sidewalk, before he could rehearse anything. "So the pill," he said. "With typical use, about seven in a hundred people a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. I didn't know that. I've been telling you it's basically perfect." A bus went by, brakes hissing. "I'm not saying it to scare you. I'm saying it because I should have known what we were actually relying on."

There was a silence on the line long enough that he watched a pigeon cross the whole clinic driveway. Then she said, "Okay. Set another alarm, then. And maybe we go to that clinic together, after your workshop."

"After my workshop," he agreed. He was still holding the card, and now he slid it into his wallet, behind his transit pass, where he would find it again on Friday morning with his notes.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The shop smelled of isopropyl alcohol and burnt coffee, and Alyssa had decided she loved that smell, though honestly she had decided a lot of things lately. She was spending her last summer before college not at the lake with Dana and Priya, the way they'd planned since eighth grade, but behind the counter of iPhix on Route 9, learning SQL from Marcus the owner because he'd mentioned once, in an offhand way she'd probably inflated in memory, that data analysis paid real money. Her mother said she was hiding. Alyssa said she was building her resume. Both could be true, but she preferred the second version, so that was the one she told.

Marcus wanted a list of customers who had never brought in a device, dead weight in his mailing list, so he could decide whether to cut them. He'd shown her the customers table and the orders table on the ancient laptop by the register, and she'd spent two evenings getting comfortable with joins. She'd even started feeling a flicker of pride, an inchoate sense that she might actually be good at this, the way she'd once thought she might be good at the violin, an episode nobody in the family mentioned anymore.

On Thursday she wrote her first version and it worked. LEFT JOIN customers to orders, and the customers with nothing came back with empty slots where their orders should have been, holes in the rows like missing teeth. Eleven names. Mrs. Okafor. The Hendersons. A guy named Ted V. with a gmail address from 2009. She printed the list, which was a mistake, because the warm paper in her hand made the names feel like more than names.

But Marcus, leaning over the register counting receipt rolls, said he only wanted the ones worth keeping, so could she narrow it to customers whose orders, if any, totaled more than zero, so he'd know who the real dead weight was versus who just hadn't come in yet this year. Sure, she said, easy. She added WHERE orders.total > 0 and ran it again.

The list shrank. Then she counted, and counted again, and the empty rows were gone. Ted V., Mrs. Okafor, the Hendersons, all eleven of them had vanished, and instead she was looking at sixty-some customers who had ordered plenty. The exact people she wasn't looking for. She said a word she'd picked up from Priya, whom she hadn't called in three weeks, or maybe it was four, the days at the shop ran together when you weren't counting them.

She stared at the query until the screen went swimmy. Somewhere in that staring, the shape of it came to her, and later she would explain it to Dana over the phone with more confidence than she'd earned: putting a condition like total > 0 on the right table in the WHERE clause took out the NULL rows, the empty ones, and once they were gone the join was acting like an inner join, which she'd learned was the plain kind, the kind that only kept matches. The quiet customers had no total at all, so the filter swallowed them along with the zeros. She moved the condition up into the ON clause instead, reran it, and the eleven names came back. She may have said "yes" out loud, alone in the shop, though in her retelling she was very cool about it.

When Marcus came back from the stockroom, she showed him both lists and told him the trick, quickly, before her nerve failed, and he nodded slowly and said, "So which ones do I cut." She looked at Ted V.'s 2009 email and thought about how a person could exist for fifteen years in a database as nothing but absence, and how the query couldn't tell you whether that absence was poverty or a move or a phone that just never broke. Maybe she was being sentimental. Maybe working with data all day was starting to desensitize her in the other direction, toward seeing people as rows, and this small resistance in her chest was the last of something worth keeping. She didn't say any of that. She had never been the eloquent one; that was Dana, whose erudition used to make teachers sit up straighter, and whom Alyssa was suddenly, specifically homesick for.

"Cut the ones with old emails," Marcus said. "Keep the rest for one more year." Alyssa saved both queries, the working one and the broken one, in a file she labeled plainly, because she wanted to remember which was which. Then she took out her phone, and before she could talk herself out of it, she dialed. Dana picked up on the second ring, and Alyssa heard lake water in the background, someone laughing, and she said, "Hey. So I did a thing today."

story:
The portfolio workshop met in the art barn at four o'clock, when the sun came through the gaps in the wall boards and laid stripes across the concrete floor. Morgan set her sketchbook on the long table and opened it to the page she had been avoiding all week: the assignment sheet. Ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement by the end of August. The instructor, Ruth, had said the theme could be anything, as long as it was a lens and not a label, and Morgan had spent three days deciding that this sentence meant nothing.

Her problem was simpler than philosophy. She wanted to do self-portraits, because faces were the only thing she could draw with any confidence, but she had tried four already and they all looked like the same girl in the same hoodie, slightly annoyed, staring out of the page. She spread the four portraits across the table and looked at them in a row, and beside her, Dev, who was building a portfolio of etchings of drowned cities, leaned over.

"They're good," he said. "But it's like the same picture four times."

"I know."

"There's this photographer," he said, pulling out his phone. "Cindy Sherman. She did Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy black-and-white photographs, all of herself, posed as characters from movies that don't exist. Imaginary ones." He turned the screen toward her: a woman in a maid's uniform looking over her shoulder, a woman in a headscarf on a lonely road, a woman in an office dress caught mid-phone-call, each one grainy and strange, like a still pulled from a film nobody had ever made.

Morgan held the phone a long time. Seventy, from one face, and none of them repeated, because each one was answering a different question about who the face belonged to. She handed it back. "The movies aren't real?"

"That's the whole thing. She made them up."

That evening, after dinner, Morgan went back to the barn alone. The screen door complained, then settled. She found a box of costumes in the prop closet from some long-ago camp musical: a raincoat, a feathered hat, a plaid scarf, a pair of white gloves gone gray at the fingertips. She carried them to the mirror by the sinks and started trying things on, and what she saw was not a costume but a story, each one suggesting a person who might have existed, a detective's assistant, a widow, a runaway with somebody's peccadilloes written all over her suitcase. She taped a sheet of tracing paper to the window and sketched the mirror instead of herself, so that the reflection was the subject and she was only the occasion.

The next two days she drew fast. A self-portrait as an astronaut, using the white gloves and a colander. A self-portrait as a stranger on a bus, done from an angle where her own chin became somebody else's jawline. She began to think the theme was identity, and wrote "IDENTITY" at the top of a planning page, and then crossed it out, because identity was the label Ruth had warned about, the kind of word that sat on a portfolio like a tarp. The lens, she decided, was closer to pretending: not who she was but how many people one face could be persuaded to become. She was still not sure whether that was the same thing as lying. Some of the drawings felt honest and some felt like a peccadillo, a small vanity, and she could not always tell which were which.

On Thursday the whole workshop did crits. Morgan tacked her five finished pieces to the corkboard wall in a row and stood back, and the other campers went quiet in a way that could portend admiration or the opposite. A girl named Priya, whose landscapes were so precise people had accused her of tracing, pointed at the bus portrait.

"Who is that?"

"Me," Morgan said. "As somebody else."

"It doesn't look like you at all."

"It's me in the mirror," Morgan said. "I just drew the reflection."

Priya frowned, then leaned close, and her frown turned into something else. "Wait. The mirror's not flat. That's why the jaw is wrong. You didn't change it. The mirror changed it."

Morgan came forward and looked, and it was true: the old mirror in the barn was warped along one edge, and every portrait she had done at that sink carried the same small distortion, a jaw pulled subtly out of true, and she had spent two days thinking she was inventing people when the glass had been inventing them with her. She laughed, and then stopped, because the question she had been carrying all week turned over and showed its other side.

"So the series is a collaboration," Dev said from the back. "You and a warped mirror."

"Then that's the statement," Morgan said, and pulled the fifth drawing off the wall and held it up to the light, running her thumb along the bent jaw. "I did all this work pretending to be other people, and the whole time the mirror was doing the pretending for me." She looked at the glass by the sinks, which gave back her own face, slightly and faithfully wrong.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The article was in German, and Payton had forty minutes to stand up in front of Frau Delgado's third-period class and summarise it aloud. She'd had the photocopy since Monday, and it was now Wednesday, and she had spent most of Tuesday evening decoding the final paragraph, where the sentences ran long and the verbs crowded toward the end where she couldn't find them. Her notebook margins were dense with translations of words like Grundwasservorkommen, which, she'd learned, meant something like a body of water held underground. An aquifer, apparently. The article was about one in the north of the country, and farmers, and a court ruling, though she couldn't yet say how the three connected.

Her problem was simpler than the language, though she didn't know that yet. Her problem was that Dana Okafor had already gone. Dana, who had spent a semester in Vienna, had stood at the front of the room yesterday, rested her hip against the whiteboard tray, and delivered a summary so smooth that Frau Delgado had stopped writing in her grade book and just listened. Today, when Frau Delgado called the roll of remaining names, Payton's was third, and there was a boy named Marcus between her and the door, which meant she couldn't leave.

"You look like you're going to a funeral," said Jia, dropping into the seat beside her. Jia was in the class for the easy credit and spent most of it drawing. Today she was drawing the back of Marcus's head.

"German funeral," Payton said.

"Is that the aquifer thing?" Jia nodded at the photocopy. "Dana did the aquifer thing yesterday. She was good."

Payton looked down at her pages. She'd highlighted the last paragraph so heavily it had gone damp and translucent. "The ending is the hardest part," she said. "I figured if I can get through the ending, the rest is easy."

Jia shrugged and went back to Marcus's head.

The first two students went. A boy summarised his article about a football match by reading the score aloud in German, which was technically a summary, and Frau Delgado's pen moved in a way that suggested it was not technically enough. Then a girl whose article was about a film festival gave a list of film titles and sat down fast.

"Payton," said Frau Delgado.

Payton stood. The room's attention arrived all at once, the way it does, and she looked at her damp paragraph and understood, with a clarity that felt almost physical, that she could not begin there. She would have to read the last paragraph aloud first, in her halting German, and everyone would wait through it, and then she would arrive at the beginning with no time left and no summary given.

So she flipped the page over and started at the beginning instead, improvising, and the first paragraph was strange. It was short. Four sentences. And it told her, before she had struggled through anything, who had sued whom, what the court had decided, and what it meant for the farms above the aquifer. It was, she realized, the whole story, compressed into four sentences she could actually read. The paragraphs after it only added detail. The paragraph she had agonized over, the one at the end, the one she had treated as the key, was the least important part on the page.

She paused long enough that Marcus looked up.

"It's like a pyramid," she said slowly, mostly to herself, and then, because she was standing at the front of a class and had to say something, she said it to them. "Inverted pyramid. The important facts are at the top, the first paragraph, and everything after is less important, details at the bottom." Her voice steadied as she said it, because the structure was holding her up. She gave the core of the article in German: the ruling, the farms, the aquifer, the year the case began. Then she added one detail from the middle, a quote from a farmer, because she had time left and it was good. Then she sat down.

Frau Delgado's pen did the thing it had done for Dana.

After class, Jia caught her in the hallway. "That was better than Dana's, actually."

"It wasn't. Dana didn't have to figure out which end of the article to read."

"That's why it was better," Jia said, but Payton was only half listening, because she was recalibrating something, the whole evening of work she'd spent on the wrong paragraph, and it bothered her in a way she couldn't settle. She'd wasted hours. But without the hours, she wouldn't have recognized the shape when she saw it. She couldn't decide whether the waste had been the point or just waste.

"You're doing the face," Jia said. "The thinking face. Stop it, we'll be late."

In the cafeteria line, Dana appeared beside her, tray first. "I heard you did the aquifer one."

"You did the aquifer one," Payton said.

"No, mine was the football match. The score one. That was me." Dana smiled a little. "I just wanted to see your face when you found out I did the film festival instead."

Payton laughed, or started to, and then stopped, because Dana was already walking away, and Payton still didn't know which of them had done what, or why it mattered that she find out. She looked down at her tray, then back up at the door Dana had gone through, and got in line for the second slice of bread.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
story:
Megan arrived at the science museum an hour before the fair opened, carrying her capacitor in a shoebox lined with paper towels. The grand hall smelled like floor wax and old rain, and above the admissions desk a suspended skeleton of a blue whale hung so low she could see the seams in its fiberglass ribs. Her table was number fourteen, between a boy with a model aquifer and a girl who had grown moss on a corkboard.

She set the plates upright on their wooden stand, twelve centimeters apart, checked the wire to the hand-crank generator, and then read the message her lab partner, Dana, had sent the night before. "Good luck today. My mom says I have to visit my aunt, so don't set anything on fire." Megan read it twice. There was no mention of coming late, or of the argument they'd had on Tuesday about whose name went first on the display card, and the absence of any mention felt louder than an apology would have. She typed "we'll be fine," deleted "we," typed "I'll be fine," deleted the whole thing, and put the phone in her pocket.

The judges came through at ten, lanyards swinging. The first one was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, who looked at the two aluminum plates and said, "Tell me what's happening in there."

Megan had rehearsed this part. "When I crank the generator, it puts a voltage across the plates," she said. "The field between them is uniform, which means it has the same strength everywhere in the middle. The electric field strength equals the voltage across the plates divided by the distance between them, E equals V over d." She pointed at the meter clipped to the stand. "Right now it reads ninety volts, and the plates are twelve centimeters apart, so the field strength is ninety divided by twelve."

"Seven point five," the judge said. "Volts per centimeter."

"Per centimeter, yes." Megan felt her ears go hot, not from embarrassment but from the small clean click of it. She had gotten the formula wrong for two weeks, multiplying instead of dividing, and had only caught it when she noticed her answers made no sense, fields getting stronger as she pulled the plates apart, which contradicted everything the museum's electrostatics exhibit downstairs had shown her, the one with the buzzing metal sphere and the girl's hair lifting off her shoulders like slow seaweed.

"So if I move the plates closer together," the judge said, "same voltage?"

"The field gets stronger. V over d, and d is smaller." Megan slid the adjustable stand until the plates were six centimeters apart, cranked until the needle settled at ninety again, and watched the woman's eyebrows rise slightly at the meter. "Fifteen now," Megan said. "Half the distance, twice the field strength."

The judge made a note on her clipboard. "You're not going to expatiate on the health effects of electric fields, are you? The last table lectured me for ten minutes."

"No," Megan said. "I looked that up. Between plates like these, at these voltages, nothing deleterious happens to you. The dangerous thing would be the discharge if I shorted it, which is why the resistor is there." She touched the small cylinder soldered across the terminals. "It drains the charge slowly."

The judge smiled at that, the way people smile when someone has answered the question behind the question, and moved on to the aquifer boy.

The hall filled slowly with families, and by noon Megan had explained the plates nineteen times. A small boy asked her whether the field was the blue stuff, and she said no, there wasn't blue stuff, the field was the name for how the space between the plates had changed, and he looked unconvinced and went to find the dinosaurs.

At one o'clock she sat behind her table and ate the sandwich she'd brought, and her phone buzzed. Dana again. "How'd it go. Are we winning." Not a question mark anywhere, Megan noticed, and no mention of the name order either, though the display card still read DANA KOWALSKI AND MEGAN PRIETO, which Megan had printed on Tuesday before the argument, in a moment of generosity she now regarded as a heuristic that had failed her, the general rule being that yielding early prevents fights, evidence here being that it hadn't.

She typed, "Judge liked it. Plates closer means stronger field, same voltage. You would've been good at the judge part." She looked at the whale ribs, at the light coming down through the glass roof in long dusty columns. Then she added, "We can talk about the card when you're back," and sent it, because she had decided during the nineteen explanations that the order of names on a card was a thing she could hold loosely, though she was not entirely sure she'd still feel that way on Monday, and she was honest enough with herself to leave that open.

Dana replied with a single thumb.

Megan put the phone face down, wiped the aluminum with her sleeve, and waited for the next family to stop.
