activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
Nathaniel had told his mother he was meeting a study group, which was true in the sense that Priya was technically a group of one, and that they would technically study, provided the museum café sold coffee strong enough to sustain the pretense. The biology placement exam was Monday. If he passed it, he'd skip the introductory lecture course and start the second-semester sequence, which mattered for reasons he hadn't explained to anyone, least of all himself.

The museum was nearly empty this late in the afternoon. Light came slantwise through the atrium glass, turning the hall crepuscular, the exhibits glowing in their cases like things underwater. Priya walked ahead of him past the dinosaur cast, past the pendulum knocking down its little pins, and stopped at a doorway marked Cells and Energy.

"Two hours," she said. "Then dinner. I'm not imputing any nobility to this. You just want to skip a class."

"I want to start where I actually am," Nathaniel said. "Not where the registrar thinks I am."

Inside, the room was dim and blue, mitochondria enlarged to the size of rowboats lining the walls. He'd read the chapter three times the night before. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: he could recite the order, could name glucose and pyruvate and the carbon dioxide that left at the end like steam from a train. What he couldn't have done, if someone put a gun to his head, was say how any of it made ATP. The textbook kept using the word "coupled," and the word sat there doing nothing, a platitude of biochemistry, as if naming a connection were the same as having one.

Priya found the interactive first. "Come look at this."

It was a model, waist-high, a housing shaped like a mushroom cap with a stalk descending into a cutaway membrane. A handle made the stalk turn. When you cranked it, three knobs at the top opened and closed like mouths, and a counter on the side tallied glowing pellets. The label read: ATP SYNTHASE. Nathaniel read the smaller text twice. Protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP. That was all. No explanation, just the sentence, and the machine waiting for him to crank it.

"It's a motor," Priya said. "Look, you turn the bottom and the top does the work."

"No," Nathaniel said slowly, and then stopped, because he wasn't sure yet what the no was doing. He'd been turning it in his head since the label. The protons weren't food or fuel the way glucose was. They were stacked up behind the membrane like water behind a dam, all those electrons from the transport chain pumping them across, and the only place they could flow back was through this one enzyme. Through it. And flowing through it made part of the enzyme spin. The spinning was the whole point. The motion itself built the ATP. He cranked the handle and watched the knobs open, close, open, each cycle adding to the counter, and something in his chest turned over with it.

"The glucose doesn't make ATP," he said. "Not directly. The glucose pays to stack the protons up. Then the protons fall through this thing and it spins and the spin makes the ATP. It's a rotary motor. Like a mill wheel, except it's making molecules."

"You just figured that out from a handle and a sign?"

He was still cranking. The counter climbed. Somewhere upstream of him, in every cell of his arms, this was happening constantly, billions of tiny motors, and he had gone eighteen years without knowing. "The chapter never said it like that. It kept saying coupled, coupled. Nobody said spin."

"Maybe that's why you failed the practice test," Priya said, and there it was, the thing he hadn't told her. She said it lightly, but she'd been carrying it all afternoon; he could hear the care under the lightness. He'd told her he'd done fine on the practice exam. He'd told his mother the same thing on the phone, standing in the kitchen with his back to her, and his mother had said that's wonderful, honey, and gone to bed early.

He let the handle slow. The counter stopped.

"I got a fifty-two," he said. "The practice test. I got a fifty-two and I told my mom I did fine."

Priya didn't answer right away. Around them the blue light pulsed in a slow rhythm, like something breathing. "Why lie to her?" she said finally. "She's not going to take the exam for you."

"Because if she thinks I'm fine, I can still decide whether I'm fine. If she knows, it becomes a thing. It becomes her worrying at the kitchen table while I'm trying to read about protons." He heard how it sounded even as he said it. He was trying to keep a version of himself intact, and the cost was that his mother was holding a fact that wasn't a fact.

"And now?"

"Now I don't know. Maybe I tell her tonight. Maybe I tell her after Monday, when I can tell her the real result instead of the practice one." He looked at the model, at the three patient mouths still half-open where he'd left them. "That's still lying by omission, isn't it."

"That's your call," Priya said. "But if you're asking me, the spin makes the ATP. The worrying doesn't make anything." She checked her phone. "Dinner. You have until the museum closes to decide."

The guard was already walking the far hall, keys sounding against his thigh. Nathaniel gave the handle one more full turn, watched the counter tick up, and let it go.

On Monday, he thought, he'd write the whole pathway out from the top: glucose, glycolysis, the cycle, the chain, the dam of protons, the motor. And tonight, probably, he'd call his mother. Probably. He took a last look at the spinning thing going still and followed Priya out through the blue room's doors.

"Order me the thing with the noodles," he called to her back. "I'll be there in a second."

He stood a moment longer in the emptying hallway, then went.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
"Okay," Anna said, spreading the two leases across the cafeteria table like a dealer laying out cards. "You are about to witness adulting."

Priya set down her milk carton. "Those are from your mom?"

"My mom photocopied them at work and left them on my bed with a sticky note that said, in all caps, YOU DECIDE." Anna smoothed the first page. "So now I decide. Apparently."

The plan was this: Anna and her mother were moving in June, and two buildings had openings. The one on Fenwick Street wanted twelve hundred dollars a month, but it was running a move-in special, one month of free rent on a twelve-month lease. The one on Corliss Avenue wanted eleven fifty, no special, no fanfare. For a week Anna had assumed Corliss was obviously cheaper, the way she assumed a lot of things, and then she'd started doing arithmetic on the back of her chemistry homework and gotten a feeling like the floor tilting.

"Utilities," Priya said, tapping the Fenwick lease. "It says here water and trash are included. That's like fifty bucks you're not paying."

"Which sounds generous until you see the Corliss one." Anna pulled the second lease forward. "Corliss includes water, trash, and gas. Fenwick makes you pay your own gas, which, in winter, ugh."

"How much is gas?"

"No idea. That's the noxious part. Not the gas itself, the not knowing. Dad says I should call the utility company and ask for an average, but calling people is my least favorite sport."

Priya grinned. "You could email."

"They don't email. They have a phone number from 1987." Anna pulled out her notebook, where she'd already started a grid in purple pen. Across the top she'd written FENWICK and CORLISS and, underneath, in smaller letters, ECON BOX, because the whole thing had started as extra credit for her economics unit. The teacher had said bring in a real-world comparison, and Anna had thought, real world? I live in the real world, my house has a for-sale sign in the yard. Now the extra credit had turned into her actual life, which felt like bringing your homework on vacation.

She wrote the Fenwick numbers first. Twelve months at twelve hundred, but one of those months was free, so eleven months actually paid. Eleven times twelve hundred. She did it twice because the first answer seemed too polite. Thirteen thousand two hundred for the whole year. Divided by twelve months, because that was the fair way to look at it, the way you'd actually live it. Eleven hundred a month. She sat back.

"That can't be right."

"What?" Priya leaned over. "What can't be right?"

"Fenwick. The expensive one. With the free month it works out to eleven hundred a month. Effective rent, it's called." Anna stared at her purple grid. "That's fifty dollars less than Corliss."

"Wait, so the move-in special beats the cheaper building?"

"By fifty dollars." Anna recalibrate d nothing, at first, because the tilting-floor feeling got worse. She had spent a week saying the Fenwick building was for people who liked flashy lobbies and overpaid for them. She'd said this out loud, at dinner, twice. "I told my mom Fenwick was a trap."

Priya was already laughing. "You told your mom. To her face."

"I used the word trap, Priya. I used the word trap."

"So you have to tell her she was right to look at it."

"No, worse. I have to tell her I was wrong, which is different, and worse." Anna flipped to the utilities section of both leases again, because there had to be a catch, and there it was, kind of: Fenwick's electric wasn't included either, and neither was Corliss's, so that was a wash, but the gas question still hung over everything like weather. If gas at Fenwick ran more than fifty dollars a month over what Corliss's included gas would have cost, then Corliss won again, and Anna was back where she started, only now she had a purple grid to prove it.

"Can I use this?" Priya pulled the notebook closer, squinting at the ECON BOX header. "My econ thing is due Friday and I was going to write about stagflation, which I do not understand even slightly."

"Stagflation is when everything costs more and nobody has jobs. Take the grid, it's yours." Anna pulled out her phone and found the utility company's ancient phone number. She looked at it for a second, the way you look at a diving board. Then Priya reached over and pressed dial.

"Hello?" Anna said, when a voice answered. "Hi. I have a question about average gas bills. It's for a very important homework assignment. And also my whole life."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
The trouble began on the first evening of the arts intensive, when the director announced that each camper would deliver a formal critique of a single painting at Saturday's exhibition, and Nathaniel understood that he did not know what the word "formal" was supposed to mean in that sentence. He had applied to the program in the Valle de Bravo because his portfolio needed figure drawings and because his mother had said a month away would be good for him. He had expected sketchbooks and canoes. He had not expected a lecture hall above the boathouse, whiteboards covered in terms like "chromatic weight" and "negative space," and a girl named Priya who took notes in two colors of ink and asked questions even the instructor paused before answering.

Priya had claimed The Two Fridas before anyone else could. She said it plainly, over rice at dinner, the way you might claim a window seat. "I'm doing the Kahlo. It's in the Museo de Arte Moderno in the city, and we see it Thursday." Nathaniel had been half in love with the painting since tenth grade, when he'd found a poster of it in a used bookstore and taped it above his desk without fully knowing why. He said none of this. He said, "That's a hard one," and Priya said, "That's why I picked it," and he spent the rest of the meal drawing tines on his fork with a thumbnail.

He chose a de Chirico instead, shadowy arcades and a distant train, and for three days he buried himself in vocabulary. He learned to describe how a composition divides the rectangle, how color advances or recedes, how an object repeated twice forces the eye to compare. The knowledge felt like a new grammar, and he liked grammar, liked the way rules could make a sentence carry more. But at night, in the bunkroom, listening to the lake water slap the dock pilings, he kept thinking of the poster above his desk, and of how none of his new words seemed to touch what the poster had done to him when he was fifteen.

There was a memory he kept circling. His grandfather, the summer before he died, had taken Nathaniel to a museum in Chicago, and they had stood in front of a Pollock for a long time while his grandfather, who repaired irrigation pumps for a living, said nothing. Finally the old man said, "I could do that," and then, after a silence, "No, I couldn't," and he had laughed, and Nathaniel had laughed, and neither of them had needed to say anything else about it. His grandfather had looked at the painting the way he looked at a broken engine, patiently, with his whole body, until it gave up what it was.

On Thursday the camp bused into the city, and the valley fell away behind them, the fields spread out on the alluvial flat where the river had spent centuries laying down its soil, and Nathaniel watched it all through the window without sketching any of it. In the museum the group moved through rooms of Orozco and Siqueiros, and Priya walked fast, ahead of everyone, a small determined figure with her notebook already open. When they turned the corner into the Kahlo room, Nathaniel felt something in his chest adjust, the way ears do when a plane descends.

He had never known the painting's size. On the poster, on his wall, it had always been intimate, the way a diary page is intimate. Here it was enormous, nearly square, about 173 centimeters on each side, he heard Priya telling a counselor, and the two seated self-portraits sat side by side filling it, dominating the whole wall. Priya kept stepping backward, back and back, nearly into a bench, to see how the two figures used the full square of the canvas, and other visitors had to part around her, and she did not appear to notice or care.

Nathaniel stood closer than she did. He looked at the hearts, at the artery that ran between the two women like a bridge or a leash, at the white dress and the Tehuana dress, at the storm sky behind them. He heard one of the other campers, Marco, who all week had been flattering every instructor within earshot, telling the counselor that the brushwork here was the finest in Mexican painting, and the counselor nodded along, and Priya, without turning, said, "He's such a sycophant," quietly, to her notebook.

She found him afterward in the courtyard, by the reflecting pool where the heat made the air undulate above the water so that the museum seemed to waver at its edges. "You've been staring at my painting all afternoon," she said, and it wasn't hostile, exactly. He said, "It was mine first. Sort of. In a way that doesn't count." She sat down on the wall beside him and said, "Then tell me one thing about it that isn't from a study guide."

He told her about his grandfather and the Pollock. He told her that the longer he studied formal analysis, the more it seemed like the grammar of a language he had been speaking without knowing it, and that he was afraid of what happened when you learned the grammar, which was that you could no longer say a sentence the old way. Priya was quiet for a moment, the pool trembling between them. "You could do the critique with me," she said. "Two people, two Fridas. The director said pairs were allowed if neither one was lazy." He said, "Which one am I?" and she said, "The one on the right, obviously," and he laughed, though he wasn't sure the joke had a floor to it.

They worked on it that night at a table in the boathouse, the lake black beyond the windows, the lamp making two shadows of each of them on the wall. They built the analysis together: the square format and how its stability argued against the violence of the exposed hearts; the way the left Frida's white dress bled into the ground while the right one's colors held; the storm sky as a field of feeling rather than weather. Priya argued the symbolism was about the divorce, about Diego cut out of the locket, and Nathaniel said maybe, but he thought the painting was also doing something the biography couldn't reach, something about watching yourself, and he couldn't yet say what. Priya wrote both positions down, side by side, in her two colors of ink, and underlined neither of them.

Saturday morning, before the room filled, they stood at the front with the projected image behind them, the double self-portrait looming square and enormous even flattened onto a screen. Priya nudged him and whispered, "You start," and Nathaniel turned to the painting instead of the audience, looked at the two women holding hands in the storm, and began.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
story:
Maria spread the practice test across the kitchen table, third cup of coffee going cold beside her, and read the same line for the fifth time: estimate the area under the curve between x equals zero and x equals four. Monday was the placement exam that would decide whether she started college calculus in the fall or spent a semester repeating what she should already know. She had drawn the curve twice, a gentle parabola rising like a hillside, and under it she had sketched rectangles, ten of them, then twenty, watching the gaps shrink.

Her younger brother Danny leaned over her shoulder on his way to the refrigerator. "What's with the jail bars."

"They're rectangles," she said. "The curve is like a roof and the rectangles are rooms underneath it. If I make enough rooms, the wasted space gets small."

"So it's never exact."

She tapped the pencil against the page. "That's the part I can't tell." The method was named for somebody, she knew that much, some dead mathematician, and the study guide mentioned him only in passing, as if everyone already knew. She copied the name onto the back of a receipt: Riemann.

At the kitchen computer, sticky with orange juice residue along the trackpad, she searched for him. The first solid result was a scan of an old textbook chapter with the sentence underlined in blue by some previous reader. She read it aloud mostly to make it real: "Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen."

"That's it?" Danny said, peeling an orange at the counter.

"That's the whole fact. A qualification paper. Not some grandiose manifesto." She liked that, actually. He had been applying for a job, more or less, and the way he chose to prove himself was to say what everyone had been doing loosely and make it precise. There was something almost humble in it, rectangles under a roof, and then a single clean claim about what happens when you let the number of rooms go on and on. She couldn't have explained the proof, but she could feel its shape, the way the answer stopped wobbling once the rectangles got thin enough.

She went back to the table and tried it herself with the parabola. Sixty rectangles took forever by hand, so she built a spreadsheet, one column for widths, one for heights, a sum at the bottom. Each time she doubled the count, the sum moved less. Two hundred rectangles. Four hundred. The number settled toward something like twenty-one and a third and then simply stopped arguing with itself. Danny drifted back over and watched the screen scroll.

"So it is exact," he said.

"It converges," she said, then heard how that sounded and laughed. "It settles down. The gaps stop mattering." She wrote the settled number at the top of her practice test and boxed it. Somewhere at the end of a long argument she couldn't follow yet, in a language she hadn't learned, that number had been waiting, and Riemann had drawn the map. She thought about texting her father, who believed any tuition money spent on pure math was evidence of a coming plutocracy where only people who could compute would eat. He would want her in something practical. She decided not to text him tonight. She would accede to one of his practical majors eventually, probably, but not before she had finished arguing with this.

The overhead light buzzed and she got up to find a quieter lamp. In the living room, her mother was half asleep in front of the news, a blanket over her knees, the same channel she left on every night like a companion. Maria stood in the doorway a moment. On Monday she would sit in a fluorescent room and shade little boxes under little hills, and somewhere behind the exam there would be a paper from 1854, a man standing before the University of Göttingen hoping to be allowed to lecture, offering rectangles as his life's evidence. She didn't know yet whether she was good at this or only stubborn. Both had gotten her this far.

She carried the lamp back to the kitchen and clipped it to the shelf above the table. Danny had left half his orange, the segments pulled apart in a fan. She ate one, wiped her fingers on her jeans, and started the next problem: a different curve this time, dipping below the axis, where the rectangles would have to mean something else.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
story:
Lea sat on a swing that didn't swing, one sneaker hooked in the wood chips, her physics workbook balanced on her knees. The formula for the field between two charged plates glared up at her, E equals V over d, and beneath it a problem asking for the field strength at a point between plates held at 340 volts, separated by 2.0 centimeters. Around her the playground did its afternoon business: a man commodifying his own patience by letting a toddler decide, at length, which slide to reject, and two women arguing near the water fountain about whether juice was basically soda.

"Seventeen thousand," she said aloud, dividing before she had fully decided to. Volts per meter. The number sat there looking both exact and completely unreal. She was supposed to imagine a field strong enough to matter, and she could not. Numbers like that came out of her pencil the way coins come out of a vending machine, and she was beginning to suspect she'd been vending nothing.

Her little brother, Theo, eleven and magnetically attached to the monkey bars, dropped into the chips beside her. "What's seventeen thousand?"

"Units I can't picture. It's the electric field between two plates."

"Plates like dinner plates?"

"Like metal plates, charged, facing each other." She paused, and then the science museum came back to her, the field trip in October, the jaundiced fluorescent lighting in the Hall of Measurement, everything the color of old paper. There had been a glass case with a replica inside: a squat brass chamber, and two horizontal metal plates, one above the other, with a little window and a sprayer. She'd stood in front of it for ten minutes because a card beside it said Robert Millikan, oil drops, and she'd thought at first it was an exhibit about cooking.

"Theo, remember the museum. The brass thing with the plates." He shrugged, so she kept going. "Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron with that. He sprayed tiny charged oil drops between two horizontal charged plates, and the electric field held them still against gravity."

"Oil? Like for a bike chain?"

"Like for a bike chain," she said. "Tiny drops, so small you'd need the microscope they had on it. Gravity pulls them down and the field holds them up, and when a drop just hangs there, not falling, that's the moment. That's what he watched for."

Theo considered this with the seriousness he usually reserved for referee calls. "So the drop's like on an invisible shelf."

She had written E equals V over d with the confidence of someone copying a recipe. Now she looked at the same letters and saw the drop, hanging in the brass chamber, gravity on one side of the ledger and the field on the other, the whole apparatus built to catch a single instant of stillness. Two ways of holding the same thing, she thought: the equation, which was clean and told her nothing, and the chamber, which was grimy with history and told her everything except the number. Somewhere between them was an understanding she could actually keep. What she couldn't yet do was say what a field was, only what it did, and she decided, provisionally, that this might be the honest position.

"It's not a shelf," she said. "A shelf would be easier. It's more like the drop is falling and being pushed up at the same time and the two exactly cancel. Nobody's holding it. That's the strange part. It looks held."

"You could do that to me," Theo said. "Charge me up and stick me between plates."

"You'd need a bigger power source than the playground has."

"Then jump off the monkey bars and I'll hover."

"You'd fall," she said, "and I'd be responsible, and Mom would have questions."

He went back to the bars. Lea turned to the blank back page of the workbook and drew two horizontal lines with a dot between them, suspended. Under the dot she wrote mg, because gravity pulls down; above it she wrote qE, and made them equal. The whole genealogy of her homework problem was suddenly visible to her, one line of it anyway: her exercise, then textbooks, then a man in a room watching oil not fall, and somewhere at the root a question about the smallest piece of charge there is. She didn't know the whole lineage and suspected it was messier than any diagram, papers she'd never read, arguments she'd never heard. She underlined qE equals mg and left the underline crooked.

She tried to get from her drawing back to her number. If the drop hung still, then the field had to be exactly as strong as her seventeen thousand volts per meter claimed, at least for whatever drop and whatever charge Millikan had used, which she hadn't been given and couldn't reconstruct. The problem in the book wanted only the arithmetic. The chamber in the museum wanted the world. She sat on the dead swing with both of them, unwilling to give up either, and no way yet to prove they were the same thing.

Then she got up, workbook under her arm, and walked over to the monkey bars, where Theo was hanging by his knees with his arms out, holding himself against gravity in the only way available to an eleven-year-old.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The argument started over the potato salad, which was how most arguments started at Uncle Dov's house, since Uncle Dov believed any table with twelve people at it was a table that could hold a debate. Liam had said, carefully, that he thought the rule against mixing meat and dairy no longer made sense as law, only as heritage, and his uncle had put down his fork with the pleasure of a man who had waited all afternoon for exactly this.

"You want to abolish a fence your grandfather kept his whole life," Uncle Dov said. "Tell me why."

"Because nobody knows what it's for anymore," Liam said, though he knew even as he said it that this was lazy, and his uncle's face showed he thought so too.

"Then you don't know the text," his uncle said. "You're arguing from ignorance and calling it modernity."

The challenge was this: Dov had to drive his mother, Liam's grandmother, to the airport by seven, so Liam had roughly ninety minutes and a stack of his grandfather's books, still shelved in the study where nobody sat anymore. Dov was a raconteur, famous in the family for turning a two-minute anecdote into a twenty-minute performance, and Liam suspected the deadline was partly theater; Dov liked pressure, liked watching people scramble. But there was a real stake too. Dov had offered, in front of everyone, to stop calling Liam's mother's kitchen "traif palace" at these gatherings if Liam could defend his position from the source itself. It was a small, cruel nickname, and Liam's mother pretended not to mind, and Liam wanted it gone.

He went to the study. The books smelled like pencil shavings. He found the Chumash with his grandfather's marginal notes, thin careful handwriting, and he started with the verse everyone started with, the one about not boiling a kid in its mother's milk. He had expected a proof text. What he found instead was his grandfather's note beside it, a single line: "Why kindness, why not purity? Rambam says cruelty. Others say separation. Which am I choosing, and why?"

Liam sat with that for a long time. His grandfather, it turned out, had asked the same question and had not fully answered it, and there was something in that which changed the shape of the argument. He copied the note onto his phone. Then he found the passage in Maimonides about the origin of the practice among idolatrous, hedonistic feasts, and next to it his grandfather had written "disputed," which meant his grandfather had not trusted it either way.

He came back to the table with the books under his arm. The cousins had drifted into the living room and the adults had cleared to coffee, but Dov was waiting, so it became a smaller audience than Liam had wanted, just his mother and his grandmother, which was somehow worse and better.

"Say it," Dov said.

"Your rule is a fence," Liam said. "Fine. But the verse itself is about a kid and its mother. It's about not taking the milk that fed an animal and using it to cook that same animal. If the rule is about cruelty, then modern farming, modern everything, changes what cruelty means. If it's about separation, about keeping categories apart, then it still applies, but then you have to defend the categories, not just the fence."

"That's not an argument," Dov said. "That's a survey."

"It's what the text gives," Liam said. "Grandpa thought so too. He wrote in the margin that he didn't know which reading he was choosing. He's the one who taught me the word for what you're doing, by the way. Exegesis means drawing the meaning out of the words and the context. Eisegesis means reading your own ideas into it. He used to say you find in a verse only what you already believed, and that's eisegesis."

Dov was quiet for a moment, and his mother, Liam's grandmother, laughed, a short dry sound. "He said that about rabbis, not about his own brother," she said.

"He said it about everyone," Dov said. He looked at the stack of books. "Including me. Fine. But you haven't resolved anything, boy. You've told me the verse is ambiguous and your grandfather was honest about it. That's not a position."

"It's the position I have," Liam said. "I think the rule still applies if the reason is separation, and I can't prove the reason. So I'm not going to say it's obsolete. I'm also not going to pretend it's obvious. The nickname still has to go."

"You'd disenfranchise a man of his best joke," Dov said, but he was already glancing at the clock, at his mother, at the coat draped over the chair by the door. He stood, and he put his hand briefly on the top book in the stack, the one with the marginal notes, and left it there a second longer than a gesture needed. "Keep the books on the shelf in the study," he said. "Not in your room. When you come back at Passover, we'll take the second half of the verse."

He was helping his mother on with her coat before Liam could answer, and at the door she turned and said, "He wrote that note the year you were born," and then Dov carried her suitcase out to the car.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
The lab smelled of wet chalk and something faintly chemical that no one could ever identify, and Maika sat at the third bench with a worksheet that had defeated her twice already. At the top, in her physics teacher's cramped hand, was the problem: a ball launched at twelve meters per second at thirty degrees, would it clear a fence three meters high? Beside her, Deniz was already on the last question, his pencil moving with the indifference of someone who had understood this weeks ago.

She had tried it the night before by treating the velocity as one thing, one arrow, one number, and the answer had come out absurd: the ball sailing over eight meters of fence or smashing into it halfway up, depending on which mistake she made. Both answers had felt wrong without her being able to say why, which was the worst kind of wrong. Now she spread the worksheet flat and started over, and Deniz glanced at her blank second page without comment, which was somehow kinder than commenting.

"The trick," he said finally, when she dropped her pencil for the third time, "is that nothing up and down ever talks to anything side to side. They're two separate problems wearing one ball."

She almost argued. It was one ball, one throw, one arc drawn on the whiteboard in the teacher's blue marker, and the whole point of the arc was that it was one continuous thing. But she copied his first line anyway: split the velocity. The vertical part was twelve times the sine of thirty degrees, which was six. Six meters per second, straight up, as if the sideways motion had never existed.

Then she stalled again, because knowing how fast it went up did not tell her how high it went, and the fence was three meters and her mother's car was parked on the other side of it, which mattered because if the ball cleared the fence it would land on the car and Maika would be paying for a windshield until graduation. She had actually volunteered to test the throw after class, since the seniors had been arguing about it since Monday, and only now did it occur to her that volunteering before solving the problem had been backwards.

She found the formula in her notes, half-buried between a failed quiz and a schedule for the debate tournament: ignoring air resistance, maximum height equals the square of the initial vertical velocity divided by twice g. Six squared was thirty-six. Twice nine point eight was nineteen point six. Thirty-six over nineteen point six. Her calculator said 1.84, and she wrote it down and then sat very still.

The fence was three meters. One point eight four was not three meters.

"So it hits the fence," Deniz said, reading her page upside down, and Maika felt a strange double reaction: the small satisfaction of the thing actually working, and the larger embarrassment of having promised a throw that physics had just quietly cancelled. She checked it again, the way she checked everything now, ever since the debate coach had told her that a position you only examined once was not a position, it was a preference. The math held. The ball would crest at one point eight four meters and come down against the chain-link like a deposition against her own confidence, a written record of the gap between what she'd assumed and what was true.

She walked to the window anyway. The fence stood out in the yard, and the seniors had left the ball on the bench outside, orange and half-deflated. Her first thought was that she could still try the throw and let everyone see the ball bounce off, which would at least be honest; her second thought was that there was no dignity in demonstrating a failure you'd already predicted on paper. Neither thought felt entirely tenable. What she actually wanted was for the answer to be wrong, and she knew that wanting was not evidence.

She went back to the bench and resuscitated her first attempt, the one from last night, turning the page over. There it was: she had used the full velocity, twelve, instead of the vertical part, as though the sideways motion could help lift the ball over. It couldn't. That was the thing she was slowly willing to accept, that the horizontal and vertical were separate the whole way up, separate the whole way down, and only ever met in the single object they jointly carried.

Then she looked at the problem line again. Twelve meters per second at thirty degrees. The launch angle wasn't fixed, she realized; the problem stated it, but the yard didn't. She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and tried forty degrees, then forty-five, and at forty-five the vertical component was eight and a half, and eight and a half squared over nineteen point six was three point six seven, which cleared three meters with room to spare. It wasn't the problem she'd been asked to solve. It was the problem she actually had.

At the window she pushed the latch and leaned out into the cold. The seniors were drifting toward the yard for the last ten minutes of lunch, and one of them, sensing something, picked up the orange ball.

"Forty-five degrees," Maika called down. "Throw it at forty-five."

"Or what?"

"Or it hits the fence." She watched him weigh the ball, step back from the chain-link, and raise his arm.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The overhead projector hummed above the third-row sinks, throwing a yellowed diagram of a mitochondrion across the whiteboard, and Tyson copied it for the third time because his first two attempts had collapsed into arrows pointing nowhere. Glycolysis he could manage: glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, a small profit of ATP, pyruvate drifting toward the mitochondrial membrane like a commuter catching the last train. After that the diagram turned into a spiral of names, citrate to isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate, and somewhere in the spiral, electrons were supposed to start their descent. He set his pencil down and rubbed the graphite smudge on the heel of his hand.

His lab partner, Priya, had already filled two pages and was now drawing little stars next to the steps she was sure would be on the exam. Her want was simple and she had announced it at nine o'clock that morning: finish the review sheet before lunch, leave school at noon, and get to the community college gym before the open tryouts closed. She had been practicing her jump shot in the parking lot before first period, and the ball was still in her backpack, wedged beside her binder so it wouldn't roll.

"You're on the Krebs cycle," she said, tapping his page. "You've drawn the same arrow four times."

"It's a cycle," Tyson said. "It goes around. I don't see how you draw something that has no beginning."

"It has a beginning. Acetyl-CoA comes in, citrate comes out."

"But why is it called the Krebs cycle? Half the words on this sheet are just people's names. Who decided a piece of your cells gets somebody's name on it?"

Priya looked at the clock, then at her stars, then at him, and he could see her weighing whether his question was worth the minutes. She flipped to the back of the textbook anyway, which surprised him. "It says here Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937," she read. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it."

"Shared," Tyson repeated. "With who?"

She ran her finger down the column. "Somebody else, for something else. It doesn't say." She closed the book on her thumb. "There. Can we finish?"

He didn't answer right away. He was looking at the diagram again, at the little wheel turning in the middle of the mitochondrion, and something about the date had snagged on him. Nineteen thirty-seven. His grandfather hadn't been born yet, and yet the wheel had been turning in every person who was alive then, every person before them, back through all of it, unnamed and unexamined until two men sat down and worked out what it was doing. The cycle hadn't needed a name to run. Only to be understood.

"I always thought of it the other way," he said slowly. "Like science invents things. Vaccines, plastics. But Krebs didn't invent this. It was already in him. In us. He just found the words for it."

"You're romanticizing," Priya said, but without much force, because she was watching his pencil start to move again, tracing glucose down through glycolysis, through the membrane, into the wheel, out along the electron transport chain to ATP. "It's a metabolic pathway. It's chemistry."

"It's both, though." He drew the spiral tighter this time, and it held. "It's chemistry that we found by asking questions, and the questions come from somewhere that isn't chemistry. Wondering isn't in the textbook." He paused, unsure of that, and said so. "Or maybe it is and I just haven't read far enough."

Mrs. Okoye passed behind them on her rounds, and Priya tried to remonstrate with her about the review sheet's length, saying it was unfair to assign twelve steps on a game day, that expecting concentration under such duress was unreasonable. Mrs. Okoye was obdurate about deadlines but not unkind; she only smiled and said the mitochondria had been working without complaint for a few billion years, which was not, Tyson thought, actually a counterargument, but which he liked anyway.

Priya finished her stars at eleven-forty and left with the ball under her arm, pausing at the door to say she hoped his wheel worked out. Tyson stayed another ten minutes, alone at the sink, redrawing the cycle one last time from memory. When he got to citrate, he wrote Krebs beside it in small letters, then Johnson under it, smaller, then sat back and looked at the two names turning inside his diagram like spokes. Somewhere across town a ball was bouncing on a gym floor, and somewhere inside his own forearm, billions of wheels were spinning without his attention, and he picked up his pencil and added the last arrow, completing the loop.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The county grant application closed at five o'clock, and by three fifteen Eve still had no list. Ms. Okafor had given her the library's member table and the checkout table that morning, along with one instruction: tell the county how many members never borrow anything, so the outreach money has a number behind it. Eve had assumed the hard part would be typing the query. She had not assumed the answer would be zero.

"Zero is wrong," said Marcus, dropping into the chair across from her at the back computer bay, near the atlases nobody touched. "Look around. Half those people are asleep. Nobody's checking anything out."

She turned the screen toward him. Her query joined members to checkouts and filtered for members whose checkout count was zero, and it returned nothing, a clean and empty grid, which was somehow worse than an error. Marcus leaned in with the confidence of someone who had finished a coding camp the previous summer and forgotten most of it.

"Your join eats them," he said, mostly to himself, scrolling through her SQL. "Before your filter even runs."

"That's not how it works," Eve said, though a cold feeling suggested otherwise. "A join just connects the tables."

They argued about it in whispers for ten minutes, the way they had argued since seventh grade, while a man at the next station asked them twice to lower their voices. The deadline sat in the corner of Eve's mind the way a test sat at the front of a classroom. She thought about the members in the database who had cards and had never once borrowed a book. Somewhere in the join, she realized, they were simply gone, and she could not say where.

"Run it without the filter," Marcus said finally. She deleted the WHERE clause, executed, and the grid filled with four hundred rows of members who had checkouts attached. She scrolled and scrolled. Her list had every active borrower in it, and none of the others. The join itself was the filter. It returned only rows that had a match in both tables, so the members with no checkouts disappeared from its results entirely, before any condition she wrote could ever find them. She sat back. All morning she had trusted the empty result as an answer instead of asking what question it was actually answering.

"LEFT JOIN," Marcus said, and she typed it before he finished the word, keeping every member from the left table whether or not a match existed, then filtering for nulls. The query ran. The number that came back was two hundred and eleven, and beneath it the names: people who had signed up at the summer fair, people who had moved, people who had apparently wanted only the quiet.

Ms. Okafor arrived at the reference desk at four forty with a folder and a pen she kept clicking. Eve printed the list and carried it over, conscious of her heartbeat, and explained what she had found: not that the library had no inactive members, but that her first query had been built in a way that could never see them. Ms. Okafor read the first page slowly. She read the second page more slowly.

"You're on here," she said.

Eve leaned over the desk. There was her own name, her own card number, in the column of members who had never borrowed anything. She had signed the form in September, the week she started volunteering, thinking she would use the library constantly. Since then she had come every Tuesday, sat at the back bay, taught herself queries, argued with Marcus, and carried every fact she needed in on her own two feet.

"Fix it," Ms. Okafor said, clicking the pen once and handing it to her. "Cross your name off. Then we'll talk about the two hundred and ten."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Nathaniel had been at his grandmother's house for three days, and the ten-minute play was due in nine, and so far he had produced a title ("The Fight") and a stage direction ("A kitchen. Evening."). His grandmother, who had spent forty years in community theater and referred to her own retirement as "between engagements," had converted the dining room table into a writer's desk by putting a vase of dandelions on it, which she called his muse.

The problem was the scene itself. It was about the night his sister Priya came home two hours late and he told their mother before she got to tell her herself, and how she'd stood in the doorway of his room afterward and said, "Nice, Nathaniel. Really nice." He had written it out faithfully, and read it back, and it was terrible. Everyone said exactly what they felt. His mother said, "I'm very angry and also worried." Priya said, "I feel betrayed by you." On the page they sounded like robots filing complaints.

His grandmother drifted past with a watering can and peered over his shoulder. "Everyone is announcing things," she said. "People don't announce. People conceal." She watered a fern that had clearly been dead since spring, then set the can down and delivered a line with sudden, alarming tenderness: "Lovely weather we're having." Then, in the same breath, flatly: "That's what I said to your grandfather the day the bank called." She picked up the can and left, which Nathaniel was beginning to understand was her version of a master class.

He sat with that. He tried writing a scene where two characters talked about the weather while meaning something else entirely, and it was worse, because he had no idea what they meant. He was a virtuoso of saying nothing, apparently, but he had no talent for meaning something. He crossed out four pages. He ate a granola bar his grandmother had bought in bulk in 2019, because she was penurious in the specific way of a person who had once been genuinely poor and now simply distrusted expiration dates.

That evening she cornered him after dinner. "Read it to me," she said, arranging herself on the sofa like a panel of judges. "All of it. Don't forestall me with excuses about drafts. A play exists when someone listens."

He read. When he got to the robot mother saying she was very angry and also worried, his grandmother winced so theatrically he worried for her face. But when he got to Priya's "Nice, Nathaniel. Really nice," she held up one hand.

"That one's real," she said. "Why?"

"Because that's what she actually said."

"And what did she mean by it?"

He thought about the doorway, the way Priya had looked at his shoes instead of his face. "Not nice things."

"So write the scene again, but take out everything they mean, and keep only what they say."

He started the rewrite that night at the kitchen table. The mother didn't say she was angry. She said, "There's leftover pasta," and put a plate in front of Priya, and stood there while Priya didn't eat it. Priya didn't say she felt betrayed. She asked Nathaniel how his history paper was going, in the tone of someone offering him one last chance to say the right thing, and he said it was going fine. Ten minutes, he realized, was almost too much time for how little people would say to each other in that kitchen. The whole fight was going to happen underneath.

The next morning he read the new version aloud to his grandmother, doing all the parts, holding the pasta plate for the mother. When he finished, she was quiet for a moment, which frightened him more than any wince.

"Say it," he said. "What's wrong with it."

"Nothing's wrong with it. I want to know what you'd call what you did. You wrote all the feeling, and then you buried it."

"Subtext," he said, surprising himself with how quickly the word arrived. "Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say. The anger and the love that the lines never name out loud." It was from a book he'd skimmed in the school library in April, a whole chapter he'd skipped because it had seemed abstract, and here it was, sitting in his grandmother's parlor in the shape of a plate of uneaten pasta.

"Love?" she said, cocking her head. "Where's the love in this scene? Nobody loves anybody in this scene."

He looked at his pages. The mother making pasta nobody asked for. Priya asking about his paper at all instead of walking past his door. Him saying "it's going fine" when the right answer, the one that might have fixed things, was "I shouldn't have told her before you could." Everyone in the scene was angry, and everyone was doing something kind, and nobody would admit either one.

"I don't know if it ends right," he said. "The real night didn't end right. Priya just went to her room."

"So let your play do the same thing," his grandmother said. "We are not in the business of fixing kitchens, dear. We're in the business of standing in the doorway."

For the staged reading, she insisted on full ceremony. She dragged the armchair to center parlor for the mother, positioned the coffee table as the counter, and cast herself as director with a pencil for a baton. "Places," she called, though the cast was one seventeen-year-old boy and a teapot. Nathaniel picked up the pasta plate, faced the armchair, and delivered his first line, which was no line at all, just a silence in which somebody, somewhere under the words, hoped to be forgiven.

His grandmother tapped the pencil against her knee. "Again," she said. "But this time, be sorrier."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
story:
The bus from campus dropped them at the edge of the memorial park just after ten, and Addison unfolded the paper her professor had photocopied for anyone who wanted the extra trip: two pages from a 1965 book called Atomic Diplomacy, by Gar Alperovitz, and beside it a paragraph from a textbook that disagreed with him. Her roommate, Priya, had come along mostly for the autumn air and the bakery near the visitors' center, and she was already eating a maple scone as they walked toward the low granite wall where the names began.

"So which one are we supposed to believe," Priya asked, brushing crumbs from her jacket, "the book or the book?"

"That's the assignment. Weigh them against the evidence." Addison had said it lightly, but she had been carrying the two excerpts around for a week like a stone in her pocket, reading them on the bus, in line at the dining hall, in bed before the lamp went off. Alperovitz argued that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. The textbook called that overreach, an argument stretched past what the documents could hold.

They stopped where the wall turned a corner and a small bronze plaque mapped the Pacific theater. An older man in a veterans' cap was standing there, squinting at it, and when Priya leaned in to look he shifted half a step aside to give them room without being asked. Addison noticed that. She noticed, too, that his hands were unsteady on his cane, and before she thought about it she said, "There's a bench in the shade, if you want it," and he thanked her in a voice like dry paper but stayed standing.

"My grandfather was on a ship headed for Japan in August of forty-five," Priya said quietly, once the man had drifted toward the wall of names. "The invasion fleet. He always said the bombs were the last act of the Second World War. They saved him."

"Alperovitz would say they were the first act of the Cold War," Addison said. "Gar Alperovitz, in Atomic Diplomacy, 1965. He argued the bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Partly. Not only."

Priya demurred, holding up one crumb-dusted finger. "Partly is a slippery word. It lets him claim everything and prove only something."

"I know." Addison sat down on the bench after all, and Priya sat beside her and split the second scone in half without comment, handing half over. The kindness of it steadied her more than she admitted. "That's actually what I keep circling. The textbook says the timing was military, that Japan was already collapsing but not surrendering, that the invasion plans were real and enormous. Alperovitz says look at who the diplomats were watching. Neither of them shows you the whole board."

The veterans' cap moved slowly along the wall, pausing at certain names. Addison watched him and found she could not summon the mild ennui that had been sitting on her all semester, that grey flattening of everything lectures had begun to produce. This was different. Two explanations, both speaking to the same August, and the evidence thin and contested and mostly locked in the heads of men who were now leaving, one by one, like the man in the cap, whose hand rose once to touch the granite and then fell back to the cane.

"You're doing the thing," Priya said. "The thing where you argue with yourself out loud and expect me to keep score."

"Keep score, then. My grandfather figure, your grandfather, the invasion fleet. That's evidence the bombings belong to the Second World War. The Soviet warning, the timing, that's evidence for Alperovitz's reading, the Cold War already starting inside the ending. Both can be true at once. A decision can have more than one reason." She turned the photocopied pages over, as if the backs might confess something, and found only library stamps.

Priya was quiet for a moment, which for her was nearly unheard. "My grandfather never talked about it like history," she said finally. "He talked about it like weather. Something that happened to him. Maybe that's the part your two historians can't get at. They're both writing about the century, and he was just standing under it."

The man in the cap had reached the end of the wall. Addison stood, gathered the papers, and walked over to ask him, before she could lose her nerve, whether he had been in the Pacific. He said he had been a radio operator, that he was seventeen then, younger than she was now, and that he did not care what the books said because he had carried the codebooks and the codebooks did not care either. Then he looked at her more closely and asked, "So what do your books say, anyway?" and Addison heard herself answer, "I don't know yet. That's what I'm trying to figure out," and he laughed, a small dry sound, and said, "Good. Keep it that way," and tapped the wall once with his cane.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
The pastry kitchen at Marchetti's smelled of burnt sugar and dish steam, and Justin had been standing over the marble slab for forty minutes, moving melted chocolate in long arcs with his offset spatula, waiting for something he could not yet name. Chef had told him only this: temper is a feeling in your wrist before it is a temperature on a thermometer. That was the kind of thing Chef said, laconic and unhelpful, and Justin, who had spent two years of chemistry class believing that anything measurable was therefore knowable, had privately decided it was contrivance, a mystique old cooks built around work that was really just numbers. He kept the thermometer clipped to the bowl anyway. Forty-five degrees down to eighty-one, seed, hold. The method was not the problem. The problem was that yesterday's test batch, the one he had cooled in the walk-in fridge and carried out to the dining room for Chef to inspect, had come back dull, its surface furred with a dry white grit like frost that would not wipe away.

"It's not ruined," said Rosa, who ran the plating station and had watched him scrape the batch into the bin. "It's just ugly."

"Ugly is ruined," Justin said. "It's supposed to snap."

He thought about it on the bus home, and again this morning while he chopped the couverture, and he had arrived at a suspicion he did not like: that the fridge was the villain. The chocolates had been cold, the dining room was heavy with July air, and somewhere between the walk-in and Chef's fingers, something had happened to the surface. He had read enough to know that fat could bloom, that gray streaks meant the cocoa butter had misbehaved. But this was not gray and it was not streaks. It was white and dry and gritty, like salt left on a window after a flood.

He worked the chocolate now, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, and the sound changed under the spatula, a thicker drag, and when he lifted a ribbon of it, it held for a moment before falling. His wrist, he noticed, had already slowed before his eyes caught anything. He hated that a little. He checked the thermometer: eighty-two. Close enough to hold. He dipped the corner of a knife and watched the film set in the warm kitchen, quick and glossy, a dark mirror.

He set six molds of dipped strawberries and bark pieces on a rack in the cool corner of the dry storage room, the way the pastry textbook actually specified, not the fridge, and then, because an experiment that only confirms what you want is barely an experiment, he put two pieces in the walk-in anyway. He labeled a scrap of parchment with a pencil stub: FRIDGE, and beneath it, MAYBE DON'T.

"What's that mean," Rosa asked, leaning in the doorway with a container of spun sugar.

"Control group," he said. "My chemistry teacher spent a whole term trying to inculcate that idea and I mostly ignored her. Apparently it stuck anyway."

Rosa snorted and went back to her station, and through the next hour the kitchen filled with the sounds of dinner prep, water at a boil, the veal shanks going in, Marisol arguing with the expediter in a mix of Spanish and kitchen English that Justin was slowly learning to parse. He tempered a second batch, watched the wrist, trusted the wrist, and told himself that trusting the wrist and watching the thermometer were not opposites. Maybe they were the same knowledge wearing different clothes. He could not have said that sentence out loud without cringing, so he kept it to himself and kept moving chocolate.

At close, the dry-storage pieces were set hard and shining, and he broke a shard of bark in half and the sound was right, a clean click like a knuckle. He carried the two fridge pieces out into the dining room, where the air hung thick and humid around the tables being reset, and held them in his palm. Within a minute, the cold surfaces sweated. He waited. Rosa came over, still in her apron, and looked at what he was showing her.

"See the grit," he said. "It's not fat bloom. It's sugar bloom. The moisture dissolves sugar on the surface, and when it dries, the sugar recrystallizes into that powdery coating." He rubbed a fingertip over it, and the grit stayed, dry and stubborn, insoluble now in a way that felt like a small punishment for his shortcut. "I chilled them, I took them out, and I made this."

"So use the dry room," Rosa said.

"I'm using the dry room. I'm saying I should have believed it the first time instead of believing the fridge would save me time." He turned the chocolate over under the dining room lights, the good side gleaming, the bad side furred white, one piece of candy holding both futures at once. He set the ruined square on the table, took the good shard back toward the kitchen, and called over his shoulder, "Save that one. I want Chef to see what not to do."

He heard Rosa laugh behind him, and the door swung shut on its spring, and he was already thinking about tomorrow's batch, wrist and thermometer, both.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
story:
I was not nervous about the placement exam, and I had not spent three days pretending to study while actually scrolling through my phone, which is what my sister claimed. What I had done was spread my materials across the kitchen table in an orderly fashion: the review packet, graph paper, a borrowed calculator, and a wooden ruler that belonged to my father's old drafting kit. The packet said a passing score would let me skip introductory calculus in the fall, which mattered to me only because Priya Nair had already tested out, and I mention that as context, not as a motive.

Priya herself was at my kitchen table, because our mothers had arranged it, not because I asked. She had founded the math club at our school and had a way of proselytizing about calculus that made you feel like a person who simply hadn't heard the good news yet. "It's not about the formulas," she said, arranging her pencils. "It's about seeing what a function is doing." I said I could see what a function was doing fine, which was true in the sense that I could look at a parabola and tell which end was up.

The problem she wrote out was a polynomial, some cubic with a coefficient I'd have to check against my memory later, and the question was to find its maximum on a given stretch of the graph. "You differentiate," she said, "and then you look for where the derivative is zero." I nodded as though this was a formality. I differentiated on my own paper, in pencil, and got something, and she leaned over and said, "You dropped a sign," and I said I hadn't, and then I looked and I had. I told her the pencil had smeared. She let that go, which I took as generosity at the time.

Here is the part I got wrong first, and I'm stating it plainly because there's no other honest way to state it. She said, "The derivative at a point equals the slope of the tangent line there." I wrote down the number I'd computed, set it against the graph, and declared that the maximum was at a spot that was, in fact, not the maximum. I was not embarrassed. I remember being entirely calm, though my sister, passing through for a glass of juice, later said I had said "whatever" four times in one minute.

Priya did not argue with me. She took my ruler instead and laid it along the curve on the graph paper, tilting it until it touched the curve at exactly one point near where I'd claimed the maximum was. "Tangent," she said. "Look at the ruler. It's climbing." The ruler was, visibly, tilted upward, climbing, and a line that is climbing has a positive slope, and she said, "Your derivative here should be positive. If you got zero, something's off." Then she slid the ruler along the curve, small movement by small movement, until the tilt flattened, until the ruler lay level, touching the curve at the true peak, and the slope of that tangent line was zero. My computed derivative at that same point was zero. The two agreed. The maximum sat right where the ruler said it did.

I checked the arithmetic and found the dropped sign had migrated, or a new one had appeared, and after correcting it my numbers matched the ruler's verdict at every point we tested. I said, "I basically had it," and Priya said nothing, and I want to be accurate: she was not effusive, she was not even particularly warm about it, and I preferred that to the alternative, though at the time I told her I appreciated her enthusiasm.

We worked through two more problems. Somewhere in the second one she mentioned that half the math club had quit by October last year, that the attrition was brutal, and that the ones who stayed were the ones who stopped trying to be right on the first try. I said the club sounded like it had a retention problem, not a math problem. She said, "Sure," and squared her graph paper against the table's edge.

What stays uncertain for me is whether I could have found the error without the ruler. I believe I would have, eventually, by checking the function's values on either side of my supposed maximum, the way the packet's second method suggested. But I had declared the wrong answer with complete confidence, and the ruler had disagreed with me, and the ruler had been right. That is a fact about the ruler and about the slope and about the tangent line, and I am leaving it as that.

Priya packed up at nine. She left the graph paper with the flattened ruler-line penciled faintly across the peak, and at the door she said, "Same time Thursday." I said I'd check my calendar, and then I sat back down and wrote Thursday on the back of the placement packet, twice, and circled one of them.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
The office smelled like toner and the faint sweetness of someone's birthday cake, three cubicles over, already reduced to crumbs on a paper plate. Faith sat at her mother's desk while her mother was in a meeting, a database textbook open beside her, because she had asked for exactly this: something to do over spring break that wasn't homework. Her mother, in a fit of either generosity or desperation, had also given her a copy of the customer orders report and said, "See if you can figure out who never ordered anything. The report says nobody. The report is wrong."

Faith liked that sentence. The report is wrong. It sounded like the beginning of a detective story, or at least the middle of one, the part where the detective already knows something the report writer doesn't. She typed her first query into the practice window, joining customers to orders, and the machine answered her in the only way it ever would: with a table, silent and certain, every customer showing a count of at least one.

She sat back. Maybe the report was right and her mother was wrong, which happened, occasionally, though never about spreadsheets. But her mother had printed a highlighted list of names, hand-verified, customers whose accounts had gone quiet for a year and who should therefore have shown nothing. Should a person be able to show nothing? Faith wondered. It seemed like the kind of thing a system ought to be able to say, and yet the query kept insisting otherwise, cheerfully, a witness with no memory of the crime.

She reread the chapter on joins, which she had skimmed the night before in an embryonic way, the way you read anything at eleven at night, understanding arriving and departing like tides. A LEFT JOIN, she gathered, kept all the customers even when there were no orders to match them. So far so good. The mystery wasn't the join. The mystery was the counting. Her report counted rows after the join, and after a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still got a row, a row the join had filled with blanks. If you counted that row, everyone had something. Her mother's highlighted names were drowning in blankness being counted as substance.

Faith tried the other count. She wrote it carefully, counting the order number column instead of counting everything, and ran it again. The table redraw itself. There, near the top, was Alderman Papers, count of zero. Then Corbett, zero. Then four more names she recognized from her mother's highlighter. The blanks, when you counted only the real order numbers, added up to nothing, which was, she thought, what nothing was supposed to do. It felt almost like a trick of grammar, like the difference between "everyone said something" and "everyone spoke," a distinction so small it could hide an entire mistaken report inside it.

Her mother came back with a paper cup of coffee and stood behind her, reading over her shoulder the way mothers do, one hand on the chair back. "So what was it?"

"After a LEFT JOIN, counting the orders column gives zero for customers without orders, but counting everything gives one, because of the blank-filled row," Faith said. "I was counting everything."

Her mother made a small sound, half laugh, half sigh of a person who had spent a morning suspecting the universe and could now go back to suspecting only software. "That's the whole report, then. That's three days of arguing with accounting." She set the coffee down without drinking it, which Faith understood to be the highest compliment available. "Can you fix the real one?"

"Probably," Faith said, though she was already less sure than the word implied. She had made one query work. She did not yet know what else the report assumed, what other quiet blanks were being counted as facts, whether the same error lived in the quarterly numbers or only here. The fix was easy; the trust was harder. She copied her query into a new file, typed her initials at the top, and paused with her fingers over the keys, wondering how many true things in the world looked exactly like this, one small counting decision, invisible until somebody asked to see the zeros.

She ran it once more before changing anything, just to watch the zeros appear again, six small integers standing in a column like evidence. Behind her, someone finally threw away the paper plate.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
story:
The community centre had the smell of floor wax and instant coffee, and the room they'd been given was spartan enough that every voice carried: folding chairs in a horseshoe, a whiteboard with half a ghosted diagram still on it, a table of borrowed civics textbooks nobody touched. Avery arrived early because the sheet she'd printed said arrive early, though it didn't say much else. Model Parliament Workshop, Tuesdays, Room B. She'd told her mother it would look good on her application. She'd told herself it would be easy, since she'd done the reading, sort of, in the car.

There were nine of them. The facilitator, a second-year university student named Priya with a clipboard and a lanyard, wrote two columns on the whiteboard and said almost nothing else, which Avery found either brilliant or negligent. The columns were headed PARLIAMENTARY and PRESIDENTIAL, and the group's job, apparently, was to fill them. A boy called Marcus, who'd introduced himself by saying he'd argued with his grandfather about this for an hour at Thanksgiving, went first. "Nobody even voted for our prime minister," he said. "I asked my grandma at her place, like, why does he get to be in charge, and she said that's just how it works. That can't be how it works."

Avery, who wanted the room to know she had prepared, sort of, said the prime minister was chosen the same way a president was, basically, except without the big national race. She heard the sentence leave her mouth and immediately disliked it, the way you dislike a text the second after you send it. Priya didn't correct her. She wrote nothing in either column and moved on, and the absence of correction was worse than correction, because now Avery couldn't tell whether she'd been right or merely ignored.

The exercise turned into an argument about removal. Marcus insisted a president could only be forced out through impeachment, which he described with more confidence than detail, and a girl in a lacrosse hoodie said no, the whole thing was that you could just vote the leader out. "You can't just vote a prime minister out," Avery said, "there's no election to lose." And then she stopped, because she was no longer sure which column she was defending, or whether the thing she'd said an hour ago in the car, underlining lines with a dying pen, had been the same thing. She could feel the two columns pulling in different directions on the whiteboard and she did not know which one she had been reading from.

During the break she went to the textbook table after all. She found the page by accident, or by something adjacent to accident, since she'd been avoiding it on purpose. The passage was short. It said that in a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election. She read it three times. Nobody voted directly for the prime minister at all, that was the whole point; the job lasted exactly as long as the legislature's confidence did, and not a day past it. Marcus had been right at his grandmother's kitchen table and hadn't known why. Avery had been wrong in a folding chair and now did. She looked up and Priya was watching her from across the room, marker uncapped, waiting to see what she'd do with it.

When they reconvened, Avery asked to go back to the whiteboard. "I got it backwards before," she said. "There's no separate popular election for the prime minister at all. The office stands or falls on the legislature's confidence. That's the difference. That's the whole difference, or the first difference, anyway." Marcus said, quietly, "So my grandma wasn't dodging the question." Priya wrote it in the parliamentary column, the exact sentence, and for the first time that afternoon the room had something on the board that was true.

Then Priya turned the clipboard around, and Avery learned what the workshop actually was. Two spots, for the provincial model parliament in the spring, chosen by the end of tonight; the rest of the Tuesdays were for the two who made it. She had prepared for a class and had been auditioning the whole time. Every confident wrong thing she'd said was on somebody's scorecard. Priya asked each of them one final question, going around the horseshoe, and when she reached Avery the question was not the one Avery had braced for. "Now that you know you were wrong," Priya said, "argue the side you argued against."

Avery stood up. The room was quiet in the way rooms get when everyone has decided at once to pay attention, and outside, someone dragged chairs across the gym floor, a long scrape that slowed and stopped. She thought of the two columns, of her grandmother's kitchen where Marcus had asked a better question than any she had asked all day, of how little she still understood about what confidence actually meant when it broke. "A prime minister never faces the voters alone," she said. "So I'll start there."
