activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
story:
The library had that smell of carpet cleaner and old glue, and Kate had claimed the carrel by the window before anyone else could, spreading out her laptop, two printed articles, and a highlighter she immediately lost in her sleeve. The assignment was due Friday: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles that answered the same question. Her question, chosen three weeks ago with more confidence than she now felt, was whether reading disability was mostly inherited or mostly made by environment. The two articles disagreed completely, which was the point of the assignment, and which was also the problem.

The first article, by a researcher named Okafor, argued from twin studies that reading disability was substantially genetic. Kate had understood about two-thirds of it, and the part she had understood had mesmerized her: identical twins raised apart, turning out to struggle with print in eerily similar ways, their vocabularies and decoding speeds tracking each other across different countries and different schools. The tables of correlations looked like weather maps of a single climate.

The second article, by a Dr. Lindqvist, was leaner and angrier. It claimed that the genetic studies overreached, that what looked heritable in childhood was largely a function of schools sorting kids into book-rich and book-poor worlds. One line had stuck with her all week: calling genetics "the last refuge of those who would rather not fund libraries."

She was stuck between them the way you get stuck between two people at a party who are both right about the other and wrong about themselves. She wrote a sentence, deleted it, wrote it again. Her friend Priya slid into the opposite chair and peered at the pages.

"Which one are you arguing for?"

"That's the thing," Kate said. "I keep flip-flopping. Okafor has the better data. Lindqvist has the better conscience."

Priya snorted. "That's a whole essay right there."

But it wasn't, and Kate knew it. A review that said "both sides have merit" was a bromide, the intellectual equivalent of a fortune cookie, and her teacher had explicitly banned the phrase "more research is needed" in any conclusion. She needed something true to say, and she didn't have it.

Priya left for class. Kate sat turning her highlighter over and over, watching the two stacks of pages as if they might speak to each other. What did researchers do, she wondered, when two studies pointed in opposite directions? Did they just take sides forever? It seemed like an obvious question, and the obviousness of it made her suspicious that someone had already asked it. She opened the library database and typed, feeling slightly absurd, reading disability genetics versus environment pooled studies.

The result that came up made her sit forward. Its title named decades of twin studies, dozens of them, and the word in the method line was one she didn't know. Meta-analysis. She read the abstract twice. Instead of one study with one sample, this paper had gathered every qualifying study on the question, dozens of separate samples, and pooled their results to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could on its own. The estimates that had looked so solid in each individual paper wobbled when set beside their neighbors. Okafor's headline number sat at the low end of the pooled range. Lindqvist's dismissal sat outside it entirely.

She found the full text through the library's journal portal and skimmed to the results, and that was when she stopped, hand still on the trackpad. The author list had three names. The second one was Okafor. The third was Lindqvist.

Kate read the acknowledgments, the author notes, the conflict-of-interest statement, anything that would explain it. There was nothing dramatic, just the ordinary machinery of scholarship: these two people who had written what looked like warring articles had, some years later, combined their data with everyone else's and written a quieter paper together saying, in effect, that the truth was smaller and harder to pin down than either of them had claimed. The pooled estimate landed between their positions, with wide uncertainty around the heritable share, and a paragraph noting that phenotypic measures of reading, the actual observed skills, couldn't cleanly separate inherited potential from accumulated environment over ten years of a child's life.

She turned in her chair and looked out the window at the parking lot, the row of scraggly birches, a bus idling. The two loud articles were still loud. The quiet one, the one that had done the boring work of gathering everything, was the one telling the truth, or something closer to it, and nobody had assigned it, and it had shown up in no one's syllabus. She wondered how often that was the shape of things: the argument you notice, and the pooling nobody notices.

She opened a new document and typed a first sentence she actually believed. "Okafor and Lindqvist disagree more with each other than either disagrees with the combined evidence." Then she paused, cursor blinking, because she had to be honest about what stayed uncertain. She didn't delete it. She wrote underneath: "The pooled estimate narrows the question without settling it."

At the next carrel over, a boy dropped an entire stack of books, and Kate looked up and laughed before she could stop herself.

"What?" he said, gathering them.

"Nothing. I just found out two people who fight about everything wrote a paper together."

"Huh," he said, and sat back down. Kate turned to her screen and began the second paragraph.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
story:
Sophie had chosen her grandmother's house because it was quiet, and quiet was what she needed, because tomorrow morning at nine she had to stand in front of a examiner she had never met and debate immigration policy for five minutes, entirely in Spanish. She had three arguments about border policy and a stack of note cards, and she had told her grandmother she was here to study, which was true in the way most convenient statements are true.

She set up at the kitchen table while her grandmother shelled peas on the porch, the screen door half-open between them. Sophie had a year of Spanish behind her, a good grade in it, and a fluency in English that she could wield like a scalpel. At school she had been the one classmates half-annoyedly lionized before debates, the girl who could take either side of an argument and win both. She had assumed, in the casual way of people who have never been tested, that the ideas would carry her through, that Spanish was just a costume her arguments could wear.

She stood up, phone timer set to five minutes, and began. "La política de inmigración debe ser más humana," she said, and then hit the first gap almost immediately. She wanted to say that the system punished people for circumstances they couldn't control. She had the word for punish. She did not have the word for circumstances, or control, or, she realized with a slow cold feeling, system.

She sat back down. She tried again, and again the sentence collapsed somewhere in the middle, this time when she reached for the idea of causality, the whole spine of her argument, the reason she could claim that policy caused suffering rather than merely coinciding with it. She knew the concept cold in English. In Spanish it simply was not there. She had read a thing on her study app last week, a linguist named Merrill Swain, something called the output hypothesis, the idea that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn. At the time she had scrolled past it, because it had seemed abstract, and now she thought: this is what it means. She had felt fluent, and fluency had been a room she'd only seen with the lights off. Every time she opened her mouth she found another wall.

There were four hours until dark, and dark was when she had promised her mother she would drive home, which made this less a study session than a countdown. She changed tactics. Instead of translating her three arguments, she rebuilt them from the Spanish she actually had, shorter sentences, simpler nouns, and where the language ran out she rerouted. She couldn't say circumstances, so she said vidas, lives, and pointed the argument at lives instead. It was clumsier. It was also, she noticed, harder to hide behind. The clause that had sounded sophisticated in English now had to earn its place or get cut.

She was halfway through a run-through, gesturing at the window, when the screen door opened and her grandmother came in with the bowl of peas and said, in Spanish, calm and unhurried, "Do you really believe that, or is it just what's easy to argue?"

Sophie's mouth stayed open. Her grandmother had lived in El Paso for forty years and had, as far as Sophie knew, a vocabulary of kitchen words and pleasantries, honed at church and the tortillería, never once deployed on her granddaughter. It had never occurred to Sophie to wonder why that was.

"Abuela. You speak it. You've been listening the whole time."

"Only some of it. The parts through the door." Her grandmother sat down across from her and pushed the bowl aside. "Again, from the top. Five minutes. And this time, when you don't know a word, don't stop. Say it wrong and keep going. That's how you find the holes."

"Para eso sirve," Sophie said slowly, half to herself, meaning that was the point of it, and then she began again, watching her grandmother's face for the flinches that would mark the gaps, because those flinches, she understood now, were a map. Two minutes in, her grandmother raised one finger at a verb Sophie had mangled, and Sophie noted it and kept moving, and when she reached the part about which arguments were truly germane to policy and which were only sentiment dressed up as reason, her grandmother nodded, once, without smiling.

"Better," her grandmother said, when the timer sounded. Then she stood, lifted the bowl of peas, and added, in English, as though it cost her nothing: "Tomorrow, after your exam, you'll call me and tell me how it went. In Spanish."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
story:
Hunter spread the two books across the kitchen table at ten o'clock on a Tuesday, one propped against the fruit bowl, the other flat under the lamp. One was by a historian named Reisman, the other by a woman named Kovac, and between them they disagreed about nearly everything, which was the whole problem, because Friday's essay asked him to decide who was right.

The disagreement itself was simple enough to state. Reisman argued that the United States had exaggerated the Soviet threat, that domestic politics and a fondness for enemies explained the Red Scare better than any real danger did. Kovac argued the danger had been real, the spy networks real, the paranoia ugly but grounded. Each had footnotes. Each had conviction. Hunter had a stack of index cards and a bag of pretzels and no idea which way to lean.

His mother came through the kitchen, still in her scrubs from a double shift, looking for the yogurt she'd hidden behind the orange juice. She taught nursing, not history, but she had opinions about essays anyway. "You're supposed to pick a side," she said, spoon in hand. "That's what the rubric wants. A thesis." What she wanted, Hunter had learned, was for him to stop worrying things past the point of usefulness, which was a habit she blamed on his father and his father blamed on her.

"I don't have a side yet. I have two books and they don't even agree on the facts."

"Then find the facts." She pointed her spoon at the library stack by the window, five more books he'd dragged home because one of his teachers had said, once, that real research meant reading against your own first impression. Hunter had been trying to do that all week, and mostly it felt like being handed two maps of the same city drawn by people who hated each other.

He went back to it after she went upstairs. Reisman's prose was turgid in places, paragraphs that circled the same claim three times before landing on it, and Hunter found himself skimming, then feeling guilty about skimming, then reading the footnotes anyway. That was where he noticed the dates. Reisman's book had come out in 1989. Kovac's had come out in 2001. He sat with that for a moment, pretzel halfway to his mouth, because it seemed to matter, though he couldn't yet say why.

He pulled the laptop over and searched. What he found sent him back to the kitchen for a legal pad, because this was the thing: the Venona decrypts, Soviet intelligence messages the US government had decrypted and finally released in 1995, had confirmed that Soviet spy networks really had operated inside the United States. Reisman had written six years before that release. He could not have seen the decrypted messages; no one outside a small circle could have. Kovac had written after, and her footnotes cited the decrypts directly, page after page of them. Hunter wrote it all down, the dates lined up in his terrible handwriting, and felt something shift that wasn't yet a conclusion but was close to one. Evidence had arrived in the middle of the argument, like a witness walking into the courtroom after the lawyers had already begun.

But it didn't settle everything, and Hunter was honest enough with himself to know it. He read Kovac's chapters again, looking for places where she leaned too hard on the new material, places where she seemed to valorize the American intelligence apparatus because it had turned out to be right about the spying. And he found a few. She had a paragraph on the Rosenbergs that read more like a verdict than an argument. Reisman, for all his blindness, had been good on the ugliness of the loyalty boards, good on careers ended by rumor, and Hunter couldn't make that disappear just because the decrypts had proven one of his premises wrong. One man being mistaken about the spy networks didn't make him mistaken about the hearings.

His father called at eleven, as he sometimes did, from his apartment across town, and Hunter told him about the essay because there was nothing else to tell him. His father wanted him to visit the following weekend, wanted it in the careful sideways way he always asked, and Hunter said maybe, and meant it, and changed the subject back to history because history was easier. He explained the problem, the two books, the release of the documents in 1995, the way the whole field had to be rewritten in the middle of some people's careers. His father said, "That's quite a bind," and then, quieter, "Some choices you make without the whole picture. Doesn't always mean you chose wrong." Hunter wasn't sure his father was talking about historians anymore. He wasn't sure he was supposed to ask.

He wrote until one in the morning, filling a page and a half with a position he could actually stand behind: that Kovac was more persuasive about the reality of the espionage and less persuasive about its meaning, that Reisman had been working blind but not dishonest, and that the part he couldn't resolve, how much fear was justified once the fear had already done its damage, he would leave unresolved in the essay and take the grade that came. It was the kind of answer that wouldn't fit neatly on a rubric. His mother would say he was overthinking it. His father would say he was thinking it exactly the right amount.

In the morning he found his mother at the table with his legal pad, reading his notes over her coffee. She didn't look up when he came in. "You didn't pick a side," she said.

"I picked what I could defend."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
story:
Sienna had requisitioned the horseradish root herself from the synagogue kitchen, signing her name in the ledger like it was an official act of state, and she carried it down the hall to the social room where her family was already claiming chairs. The rabbi had told her in March that the congregation rented out the room for family seders and that this year, if she wanted, hers could be one of them. She had said yes before she fully understood what she was agreeing to, which was everything: the candles, the four questions, the timing of the meal, the whole arc of the evening running through her hands instead of her grandfather's.

Her grandfather arrived in his good coat, moving slowly, and took the seat at the far end with the air of a retired general attending a parade someone else was commanding. He had led the seder for thirty-one years. Last spring, in the hospital, he had gripped her wrist and said, "You'll do it next year," and she had nodded, and then spent eleven months not thinking about what the nod meant.

There was also the matter of Danny. Her cousin Mara had brought him, a tall boy from her dorm who was, as far as Sienna could tell, the first person at a seder in this family's history who had no idea what was happening. He sat with his chair a little too far from the table, like a man at the edge of a pool, and when the Haggadot came out he turned his over twice, front and back, as if the instructions might be printed somewhere less obvious.

Sienna lit the candles and said the blessing, and her voice cracked on the second word, and her Aunt Ruth looked at her shoes, and then it was fine. She moved them through the first cup, through the hand-washing, through the breaking of the middle matzah, and she noticed something she had never noticed as a child at this table: the seder was not one thing but many small things, each one a door, and the leader's job was to hold them all open at once without letting any of them slam.

Danny leaned toward Mara. "Why is there a shank bone," he whispered, "and what is that green stuff?"

"It's horseradish," Sienna said, loud enough for the whole table, because she had decided an hour ago that she was not going to let anyone sit through this as a stranger. "It goes on the Seder plate, and we call it maror. We eat the bitter herbs on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt." She held up the root she had signed for, its skin dull and rough. "It's not an accident that it burns. That's the point of it."

"You eat something bitter on purpose," Danny said.

"That's the whole ceremony in one sentence," her grandfather said from the far end, and it was the first thing he had said all night, and Sienna couldn't tell from his voice whether it was praise.

They got to the maror later, after the Hillel sandwich, and she portioned it out carefully, a little less for the younger cousins, and watched Danny take his first bite. His eyes watered instantly. He turned a shade of red she associated with sunburn, drank half his cup of grape juice in one pull, and then laughed, a surprised bark of a laugh that made her seven-year-old cousin laugh too, and then everyone, and her Uncle Mark said in a thick voice, "That stuff turns a man bellicose," and raised his cup like he was toasting a battlefield.

The meal came and went, the food passing hand over hand, and Sienna found herself sitting beside her grandfather during the search for the afikoman, which her youngest cousin had hidden so badly it was visible from across the room. Everyone pretended not to see it. That, Sienna thought, might be the oldest tradition of all.

"You kept the Hebrew slow," her grandfather said quietly, while the kids negotiated the ransom. "Good. Slow is respectful."

"You would have gone slower."

"I would have gone differently. Not better." He tore a piece of matzah and didn't eat it, just held it. "You argue with the text. I saw it, when you read the four questions. You read them like you were asking them, not reciting them. That's a different way than mine."

"Yours was the right way for thirty-one years."

"It was my way." He set the matzah down. "Your grandmother used to say the seder was hermeneutics you could eat. Every food on that plate is an interpretation. You added one tonight, with the boy."

Sienna looked down the table at Danny, who was now explaining to her little cousin, with total confidence and several wrong details, why everyone had eaten horseradish on purpose, and the cousin was correcting him, and Mara was laughing into her napkin. The candlelight caught the Seder plate, the shank bone, the egg, the charoset, the small pile of maror still waiting for whoever wanted more bitterness.

She didn't know yet whether she would lead it again next year, or whether her grandfather would take it back, or whether it would be some arrangement between them she couldn't yet imagine. She poured the third cup and stood, and tapped her spoon against her glass, and the room quieted and turned toward her, all of them, her grandfather too.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
The cones in the church parking lot had been Grandpa's idea, set out with a tape measure to the exact length of the testing space, fourteen paces he counted aloud each morning as though the number might change overnight. Michael had failed the test once already, in March, for a parallel park so crooked the examiner had leaned out the window to check whether the tires were still touching the curb's country. His father's response had been a lecture about humility and practice, delivered across the dinner table with the flat certainty of a man who had not sat behind a wheel of any kind since selling the station wagon. His grandfather's response was the cones.

"Hands at nine and three," Grandpa said from the passenger seat, one hand braced on the dash, the other resting on the cane he now carried even to the mailbox. "Back in until you can see the cone in your rear window at the corner. Then turn the other way. It's geometry, not luck."

Michael did it, clipped a cone, did it again, and on the fourth attempt slid between the markers with a margin he could measure in inches. He sat there with the engine idling, pleased in a way he tried to keep off his face, because Grandpa distrusted visible pride almost as much as he distrusted broccoli.

"The highway tomorrow, then," Grandpa said. "Route 9. You can't pass the test without the merge, and you can't merge in a parking lot."

Here was where the two voices in Michael's life diverged. His father believed speed was the enemy, that caution was a virtue that could never be excessive, that the safest car was a slow car. His grandfather had driven trucks for thirty years and held the opposite conviction with the same certainty: that on a highway, hesitation was the danger. For a week Michael had carried both opinions without trying to reconcile them, the way he carried his father's worry and his grandfather's calm, as if he had to choose a side eventually.

Route 9's on-ramp was short and curved uphill, and the first time Michael reached it he did what his father would have wanted. He eased off, hovered at forty, waited for a gap so enormous that no car would ever need to acknowledge him. Behind him a pickup closed fast, its driver's hand appearing on the horn, and Michael watched the traffic ahead brake, one car after another, ripple after ripple, a chain of red he seemed to have caused from a lane where he technically hadn't been driving yet. He aborted onto the shoulder, heart drumming, and put on his hazards.

"That's the fear talking," Grandpa said. Not unkindly.

"I was being careful."

"You were being slow, and everyone had to brake for you." Grandpa looked at the mirror, then at Michael. "The ramp gives you the acceleration lane so you can come up to the speed of the traffic before you move over. You weren't careful. You were a rock in a stream."

Michael sat with that. It ran against everything his father had said, and yet the braking cars were a fact, visible and unarguable, still unwinding down the highway ahead of them. He thought of how his father called defensive driving a tautological thing, safe driving is driving safely, as if the phrase closed the argument by itself. But the stream had shown him otherwise. He breathed out, checked the mirror, and pulled back onto the ramp.

The second merge was not graceful. He accelerated hard, harder than felt polite, watching the speedometer climb toward sixty while his instincts shouted that this was recklessness, that his father would have closed his eyes. Then he signaled, glanced, and slid into the stream of traffic at nearly its own speed, and nothing braked. Nothing honked. The cars simply continued, and he was among them, moving with them, one pulse in a larger rhythm. It captivated him, that sudden harmony, the way thirty strangers accommodated him without a single one of them having to slow down. Being safe, he understood now, was not the same as being slow; sometimes the careful thing and the fast thing were the same thing. His father would not agree, and Michael could not say which of them was more right, only that the braking cars had been real and so was this.

"That's it," Grandpa said quietly. "That's the whole thing."

They drove ten miles north, past the quarry and the orchards, and Grandpa talked about hauling produce on this road when the orchards were twice the size, pointing out a diner that had burned down in 1987 and a hillside where, he said, he'd once seen a mountain lion, though he then admitted he might be thinking of a different hillside, or possibly a different state. It was like this more often now, Michael had noticed, small slips in the weave, a name reached for and recovered a beat late. Some synchronicity of memory and road, both wearing down together, and Michael drove carefully in both senses, steering around the potholes and around the gaps.

Back home, the parallel park between the cones was clean on the first try, and Michael left the engine running while Grandpa worked his cane out the door. "Test is Tuesday," Michael called after him. "Want me to drive you to your appointment Thursday?"

Grandpa paused on the sidewalk, weighing it, the way he weighed everything now. "All right," he said. "But take Route 9. I like the merge."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
story:
Matthew had taped the inflation graph to the refrigerator because the kitchen was the one room where he could not escape it. The line crawled upward through the seventies, then stood at its summit, then plunged, and next to the plunge he had written, in pencil, "why?" His study partner, Priya, was coming over at seven, and their economics teacher had promised that whoever could explain that steep drop would not have to take Friday's quiz.

Priya arrived with her own agenda, which she announced before her coat was off. "I need this quiz exemption," she said. "Not want. Need. If I ace this unit, Ms. Ferrar writes my recommendation letter, and if she writes it, I'm applying early decision, and if I'm applying early decision, I need October free for essays." She spread her notes on the kitchen table and began to collate them, matching the pages from the textbook with the pages from her own binder, tapping each pair into a neat stack. "So. The line. Tell me about the line."

He sat across from her and made himself trace it out loud. "Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," he said, running his finger along the summit. "And by 1983 it was below 3 percent. Same country, same people, same stores. Three years, and the thing just falls." He looked at her. "Doesn't that seem fast? Like a fever breaking overnight."

"Explain it, then. That's the assignment."

He had a half-answer, the one the textbook kept circling. "The Federal Reserve raised interest rates. Sharply." He said the words and watched her face to see whether they landed as explanation or as incantation. She waited, chin on her fist, which meant they had not landed.

In the doorway his mother appeared, still in her lab coat, holding a mug. She was a geneticist and had a habit of listening to whatever crossed the kitchen whether or not it concerned her. "Sorry," she said. "Carry on. I'm just curious." She stayed, and Matthew found that this helped, in a strange way, because explaining to two people forced him to be slower.

He tried it as a story about restraint. "Imagine money as something that can be cheap or expensive," he said. "If the Fed makes it expensive, that changes what people do." But even as he said it, he heard the softness of it. Expensive money changing behavior was not the same as showing Priya the mechanism, and he did not actually have the mechanism. He had a fact and a sequence: rates went up sharply, and inflation, which had peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980, was below 3 percent by 1983. He had the before and the after, and a gap in the middle shaped like the word "because."

"Is that enough?" Priya asked. "Rates up, inflation down, three years. Maybe that's all the assignment wants."

"I don't think it's all I want," Matthew said. "The two things happened in that order, but I can't see the wire between them. It's like," and he looked at the graph, at the scatter of small quarterly points around the main line, "like an archipelago. You can hop from island to island and it looks like a path, but underneath there might be one landmass or there might be nothing connected at all."

His mother set down her mug. "We argue about that constantly in my field," she said. "Two populations look different, and everyone wants to say the difference is genetic, but half the time the phenotypic variation is mostly environment, and you can't tell which from looking." She smiled at their expressions. "Carry on. I just like hearing you two argue."

Priya had stopped taking notes. "So we present it as what we know and what we don't?"

Matthew pulled the graph off the refrigerator and laid it flat between them, the pencil "why?" still visible beside the drop. "We present the whole thing. Rates up sharply, then the fall. Fourteen point eight in March 1980, under three by 1983. And then we say the part everyone skips: here is the order of events, and here is where our seeing ends." He tapped the empty space under the line. "Ms. Ferrar said the exemption was for whoever could explain the drop. Maybe the honest version is the better explanation. Or maybe we lose the exemption to somebody with a smoother story."

Priya picked up her pen and wrote across the top of her collated stack: known, sequence, unknown. "Fine," she said. "But if you're wrong and I have to take Friday's quiz, you're quizzing me Thursday night."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
Let me be clear from the start: I was not failing chemistry. I had a 71, which on my scale is a work in progress, and anyway Mr. Kwan never called home, so the whole thing with my mother was an overreaction. That is the version I intend to defend, and I am aware that Priya would roll her eyes at it, since she was there.

The lab had that afternoon smell of alcohol lamps and somebody's burned pretzel from the vending machine. We were doing stoichiometry, which Priya kept pronouncing like it was a town in Romania. The problem on the board gave us a mass of reactant and asked for the moles of product, and the path ran through molar mass, which is where I always stumbled. You divide the grams by the grams-per-mole and get moles, and then you can climb the balanced equation like a ladder, and I could do each rung alone but not in sequence. That day it mattered, because the unit test was Friday, and because Priya had said, in the parking lot, "If you fail this I'm not tutoring you again," and I had laughed like it was funny.

Mr. Kwan, who does not explain things so much as scatter clues, wrote a number on the board and drew a box around it: 22.4. "You'll want this for the gas questions," he said, and moved on to take attendance, which is very like him.

"Twenty-two point four what?" I asked Priya.

"Litres. For a mole of gas." She was already three steps ahead in her notebook. "One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure. It's on the reference sheet, you don't even have to memorize it."

I said "obviously" and wrote it down, and here is the first place I have to be honest: it meant nothing to me. It sat on my page like a phone number for a person I would never call. I did the practice problem, got the moles, then multiplied by 22.4 like she did, and produced some litres of carbon dioxide, and Mr. Kwan put a check next to my name, and I felt like a fraud, because the check had no idea I was copying a rhythm without hearing the song.

That night I decided to prove something, though at the time I told myself I was just studying. I found a cardboard box in the garage, the kind my father's parts come in, and I did the arithmetic: if one mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, then a box that size was one mole of gas, sitting there, invisible. Twenty-two point four litres. I measured it out with the kitchen measuring cup and a marking pen, cut nothing, taped nothing, just drew the volume on the cardboard's inside walls, and then I sat inside the box. My knees didn't fit. A mole of nitrogen, a mole of oxygen, the whole sky's smallest unit of it, was smaller than my folded legs.

My older sister Dana found me there and stood in the doorway with her cereal. "Are you eulogizing a box?" she asked.

"I'm learning chemistry."

"You're doing existentialism in a box." She sat down on the concrete, though, which for Dana is a compliment. "So how much air is that?"

"One mole. Of an ideal gas. At zero degrees and one atmosphere." I said it the way you recite an address until it belongs to you, and I watched her nod slowly, and something in me turned over. The number had been quiescent all day, folded up on my page, and now it was the size of a box I was physically sitting in. A mole wasn't a number anymore. It was a thing you could occupy.

Which brings me to the twist, and the part I have been arranging carefully all along. On Friday I got an 88, and I told everyone the box did it, and that is mostly true. But here is what I left out: Thursday night I redid every practice problem from the beginning, and I found that on Wednesday's quiz I had used the molar mass backwards, multiplying when I should have divided, and that my 71 had been riding on that one flipped operation the whole time. Mr. Kwan had written "see me" on it in red, and I had told everyone he wrote "nice work." So no, I was not failing, and no, I was not fine. Both had been true, which is the part I'm still working on.

In the lab on Monday, Priya slid my quiz across the table and pointed at the last question, the gas one. "Explain it," she said. Not asked. Demanded, in the way she does, chin on her fist.

I took out a scrap paper and drew a box, labeled it 22.4 litres, wrote "one mole, 0 degrees, 1 atmosphere" underneath, and turned it toward her. "The grams of the reactant, divided by the molar mass, that's your moles. Then the moles of gas, that's just boxes. This many boxes' worth of gas." I tapped the drawing. "That's the whole problem. It's boxes."

Priya looked at the box for a long second, then at me, then started copying it into her notes.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
James arrived at Miss Aldana's studio with the score of Mozart's K. 333 spread across the music rack of the second piano, the one nobody played, so he could look at it while she talked. She had given him three colored pencils on Monday and a single instruction: mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation by Thursday. He had not slept well over it. The exposition he had found easily enough, and the development was chaos he could feel in his hands, but the line between the first theme and whatever came after it kept moving every time he sat back down at his desk at home.

"Show me what you have," Miss Aldana said, pulling her chair beside him. The studio smelled faintly of resin and old coffee. Through the window, a neighbor's sprinkler ticked across a lawn in slow arcs.

James pointed to measure 22, where his blue pencil had drawn a wavering bracket. "First theme ends here. I think."

"You've crossed that out twice."

"I know." He turned the pencil in his fingers. "It's tuneful all the way to 28. Why would Mozart stop a theme and then keep singing?"

"Sing it for me," she said. "From measure 15. Don't watch the pencil, watch your ear."

He played, and at measure 22 something happened that he had not noticed at home, where he'd been reading silently. The right hand stopped singing and started running. Rapid sixteenths, scales stacking on scales, no tune to hold onto, just motion. His hands slowed. "It got busy," he said. "That's different."

She waited. She was good at waiting; she folded her hands and let the silence do its work, which James found both maddening and, eventually, useful.

He played measure 22 again, then 23, then let the passage run to its end, and somewhere in there the harmony shifted under him, a small tilt, like a floor settling. He stopped and squinted at the key signature. The second theme began in a key that was not the first theme's key. He'd known that abstractly, the way he knew that water froze at zero, without ever having watched a lake.

"So the bridge," he said slowly, "the transition, whatever it's called, it's this busy part that gets you from the home key to the second key." He heard the sentence come out of himself and checked it against the page. The busier, less tuneful passage sat exactly between the two keys, exactly where his wavering bracket had been. "I couldn't find the end of the first theme because I was looking for the tune to stop. It doesn't stop. It gets replaced by traffic."

Miss Aldana smiled at "traffic" but didn't correct it, which meant it was allowed to stand.

He erased his old marks and drew the blue bracket clean and certain at measure 22, then looked at what he'd written in the margin that morning: not sure, maybe wrong, ask M.A. It embarrassed him a little, the archaeology of his own doubt, each crossed-out guess a small artifact. He had spent an hour trying to exhume certainty from a place where there hadn't been any, instead of going back to the piano and listening.

The lesson continued. The development section, when he played it, took his themes apart like someone dismantling a bicycle to see the gears, and he lost his way twice and had to restart. Miss Aldana made him find the recapitulation without looking. "Where does the first theme come home?" she asked, and he played until the familiar tune surfaced again, and it was the same tune and not the same, and the second theme arrived in the home key this time, which he only noticed because he was now listening for keys the way he listened for footsteps in a hallway.

"You're counting externality now," he said afterward, trying to explain it to her, and she raised an eyebrow, so he tried again. "Like, when I played before, the notes were the whole world. Now every modulation feels like it costs something somewhere else. It's not just Mozart's problem, the key change. It's mine. I have to follow it."

"That's not quite what externality means," she said, "but I like the misuse, so I won't fight you for it."

He laughed, and gathered his pencils, and copied his bracket and notes into a fresh page so the score would be clean for his lesson next week. He wanted the work to look effortless, which he understood, dimly, was a kind of vanity, an ascetic discipline of appearances. He could admit that to himself, at least.

At the door she said, "For next week, K. 309. Mark the same three sections."

"Is the bridge in the same place?"

"Listen for the busy part," she said, and turned back to her coffee.

He rode home with the new score unopened in his backpack and the old certainty already loosening. That evening he sat at the kitchen table and began K. 309, found the first theme, hummed it twice, and then set his pencil at the spot where the tune gave way to running sixteenths, exactly like before, and drew the bracket without playing a single note.

The next afternoon Miss Aldana played the opening for him, and the second theme arrived in the same key as the first, no new key at all, and his clean bracket sat on the page marking the boundary of something Mozart had not done.

"What do I do," James said, "if it just doesn't change key there?"

"What do you hear?" she said, and put her hands in her lap, and waited.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
Violet had claimed the last carrel by the microfilm cabinets, the one with a lamp that buzzed when she touched the switch, and she spread her photocopied pages across it like evidence at a trial. The assignment sheet said six pages, an argument, footnotes, a bibliography in Chicago style, and it was due in nine days. Her topic, whether the city had been right to close two branch libraries the previous spring, had seemed sturdy in August and now felt like a chair missing a leg. She had eleven sources, three of which disagreed with her, and no idea how to make them stand in a line.

The trouble revealed itself in the old city council minutes, a bound volume so fragile the librarian had to requisition it from the closed stacks, carrying it out on a green foam cradle as though it were an injured bird. Violet turned to the pages from the closure hearing and found her argument hiding there in plain words, but when she tried to set it down she could not decide how much belonged to the source and how much to her. In the margins of a journal article she was also using, the author's footnotes marched down the page, and at the third one the word simply appeared: Ibid. Then again, two notes later, Ibid., 114. She had never seen it before. It looked like a typo, or a password, or something the author had fallen into by accident, and she copied it onto her palm in ballpoint because she did not want to forget the shape of it.

Across the room, at the table with the outlets, Marcus was watching her watch the copier. He had been there since four, charging his phone and pretending to work on his college essay, which was due in eleven days and currently consisted of a title and one sentence he hated. His real errand was different: Mrs. Okafor had promised to sign his volunteer paperwork if he reshelved two carts, and he had reshelved the carts, but she had gone into a meeting, and now he was waiting, and the waiting had curdled into a soft gray ennui he recognized from every Sunday of his life. The girl at the carrel kept glancing at her own hand as though it held something.

He drifted over on the pretext of the copier, which was jammed, and which he had unjamamed twice before and could unjam again. "You've got ink on your face," he said, which was true, because she had rested her chin in her palm.

"Ibid," Violet said, showing him the word smudged on her skin. "Do you know what it means? It's all over this article."

"Ibid," Marcus repeated, and then, because his mother taught Latin at the middle school and it had soaked into him the way other kids got their parents' religion, he said, "It's short for ibidem. Latin. 'In the same place.' It means you're citing the same source as the note right before it." He said it the way he'd say a phone number, and Violet looked back at the page and saw the pattern unlock itself: the full citation once, and then the same book, again and again, summoned by five letters.

"Wait," she said. "So the author used one book for that whole argument." The thought arrived slowly and then all at once: the disagreement she had sensed in her sources was not just noise to be managed but the actual material of the paper. The councilwoman who called the branches "redundant" had relied on one consultant's report; the residents' association had relied on circulation numbers from the library system itself. She could put them in footnotes, side by side, and let the notes do the arguing. She wrote Ibid on a fresh index card and underlined it, feeling as though she had been handed a judicious little tool, small and exact, for keeping track of who had said what without saying it all over again.

Marcus unjammed the copier with a pencil and stayed to watch her arrange the index cards into rows, because her focus was more interesting than his essay. "So are you for the closures or against?" he asked, and Violet considered the question honestly. She had started against, mostly because her grandmother had worked at one of the closed branches, but the consultant's report was not stupid, and the numbers were not lies, and she suspected the truth was that the city had been neither cruel nor wise but merely broke. "I think I'm for the closures being wrong in a specific way," she said, "and I don't know how to footnote the part I'm still unsure about."

Mrs. Okafor came out of her meeting at six with her lanyard still twisted from her cardigan and found Marcus by the copier and the girl with ink on her face, both of them laughing about something written on an index card. She signed his paperwork against the returns desk, pressing hard with her pen, and then walked past the carrel on her way to lock the special collections room. The bound volume of minutes sat open on its foam cradle, and beside it a draft first paragraph had begun to exist in blue ink, with a small number one floating at the end of its last sentence like a held breath. At the bottom of the page, where the note would go, Violet had written the full citation once, carefully, and under it, experimentally, in letters that grew more confident as they went: Ibid., 22.

Charles had promised his mother he would stay out of the way, and for the first hour he managed it, reading in the empty corner desk by the window while her office filled and emptied around him like a tide. Then Dipa from the fact-checking desk came by with two coffees, set one beside his book without being asked, and lingered, because Dipa never simply did one thing at a time. On her screen, propped open beside his elbow, a video was playing: floodwater rolling through a town, a rescue boat, a man on a roof waving a white sheet.

"Six thousand shares this morning," she said. "People are saying it's from the river town that flooded last night."

"Is it?"

"That's the question, isn't it." She tilted the laptop toward him. "Want to see how we ask it?"

He pulled his chair over. Dipa clicked a small icon at the top of her browser, dropped the video link into a box, and let it run. The screen divided into a grid of still pictures, one after another, as if the video had been laid out flat like cards on a table.

"Key frames," she said. "It's called InVID-WeVerify." She tapped a frame showing the roof and the man. "Now we search this one backwards."

Charles watched the image travel out into the web and come back carrying pages, dates, other versions of itself. The oldest result was from two years ago, a different river, a different country, though the man on the roof had the same white sheet, the same wave. The flood in the video was real; it just was not the flood everyone said it was.

"Eighteen thousand shares now," Dipa said, and drank her coffee. "Care to write it up with me? I'll let you do the screenshots."

He did the screenshots. He cropped the frames, lined up the dates, and drafted the correction, and when he showed it to her she crossed out his first sentence, which had called the sharers careless, and wrote "hurried and afraid for a real town" above it in pencil. "The people passing it around aren't lying," she said. "They care about the right thing in the wrong direction. Only the account that first relabeled it is prevaricating, and we can't even prove that's intentional." Charles thought about that while he retyped the sentence. He had wanted the story to have a villain. The truth was more alluvial than that, deposited in layers, the original video at the bottom, the false label sifted over it by hands that might have believed what they were spreading.

At lunch his mother came to find them and read the draft standing up, one hand on the back of Charles's chair, and he felt her thumb rest briefly against his shoulder, a small pressure that meant she had noticed he had not eaten. "Take the boy to the canteen," she told Dipa, "before he eats the correction." In the queue Charles found himself explaining the plugin to a colleague of his mother's, a man named Roufik who handled climate data. "So one viral video, checked frame by frame," Roufik said. "Is that rigorous, or is it synecdoche? You prove one clip false and people conclude the whole flood is fake." Charles had not thought of that. He turned it over through his sandwich. A false video did not mean a false flood; the river town had actually flooded, and the fake clip made it harder, not easier, to believe the true ones.

After lunch he went back alone and ran the plugin himself on a second video, a warehouse fire that half his own group chat had forwarded that morning, some with angry captions, one with three exclamation marks. He dropped in the link, watched the frames fan out, picked the clearest one, and searched. The earliest version carried a date eight months old and a city four hundred miles from the one being claimed. He sat with that for a while. Two of the people who had shared it were his closest friends. One of them had lost a job last year and distrusted every official statement on principle; the other wanted, more than anything, to be first to know things. He could not correct them both the same way, and he was not sure yet what he would say at all. He only knew that the old video would not be getting any further through him.

He typed a message, deleted it, typed another. Before he pressed send he ran the frame search one more time, on a different key frame, just to be sure, and the same date came back, patient and unchanged.

Dipa leaned over his shoulder. "Still going?"

"Still going," Charles said, and hit send.
